title: Where was Dune filmed? Shooting locations in Jordan and Budapest
body:
The sweeping landscapes of Jordan, including the Wadi Rum were used for the film sequel based on the Frank Herbert novel

Dune: Part Two, the sequel to Denis Villeneuve’s 2021 sci-fi blockbuster released in UK cinemas on 1 March, was filmed in various locations across Jordan, Hungary, Italy and Abu Dhabi.

The film, based as its predecessor was, on the 60s Frank Herbert novel and set in the fictional desert planet of Arrakis, features a star-studded cast including Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, Rebecca Ferguson, Austin Butler, Florence Pugh, Josh Brolin, Javier Bardem, Stellan Skarsgård and Christopher Walken.

In its opening weekend, it reached a whopping $178.5m (about £139m) globally at the box office.

Dune: Part One raked in a total of $400m (£317m) at the box office, as well as 10 Oscar nominations after its release three years ago.

Read on for everything we know about where both Dune movies were filmed and the cast of Dune: Part Two.

Dune: Part Two is reported to have used 40 per cent more sets than the first instalment, as well as filming on location in Italy, Abu Dhabi and Jordan.

The sprawling landscapes of Jordan, which were also used extensively in Part One, provided numerous backdrops for the sequel, including Wadi Rum, the Unesco World Heritage site also known as Valley of the Moon, and the Al-Siq gorge near Wadi Araba.

Liwa Oasis, which lies on the edge of Rub’ Al Khali – the world’s largest stretch of uninterrupted desert – about 150 kilometres south-west of Abu Dhabi and four hours’ drive from Dubai, was a new spot for Dune: Part Two. Filmmakers said the desert “influenced the way we shot the movie tremendously” as well as serving as a filming location itself.

Setting the scene for the battles between the Fremen and Harkonnen, the Origo Film Studios in Budapest, Hungary also helped provide the backdrop for the film.

Like the film that came after it, Dune: Part One used the vast deserts of Jordan, Abdu Dhabi and studio locations in Budapest.

While being the first instalment in the film series to use Jordan’s Wadi Rum valley, it is far from the only Hollywood blockbuster to do so. The desert has been used by filmmakers at the helm of Lawrence of Arabia, Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker and Transformers.

Unlike Dune: Part Two, its prequel also made use of the cold landscapes of Stadlandet, Norway to provide the backdrop for The House Atreides homeworld of Caladan.

Returning to centre stage for the sequel, Timothée Chalamet (Call Me By Your Name, Wonka) and Zendaya (Euphoria, Spiderman: Homecoming) play Duke Paul-Muad’Dib Atreides and Chani.

The film’s plot revolves closely around the characters’ love story with the last duke of the noble house of Atreides falling for the the fierce female Fremen warrior Chani – as the two begin to contemplate a rebellion.

Denis Villeneuve, the film’s director, said the real-life chemistry between the actors meant the pair “were not afraid” to tackle the more “intimate” scenes in the film.

“When we did Part One,” Mr Villeneuve told Deadline.com, “I remember that very quickly there was chemistry… between both actors.

“And that in between when we were doing the promotional tour of Part One, they became real friends.

“And that, of course, tremendously helped me because the whole movie is based on their love story.”

Also returning for part two, Lady Jessica, played by Rebecca Ferguson who starred in Mission Impossible and Fallout becomes a Reverend Mother among the Fremen having drunk the mind-altering poison called Water of Life.

Josh Brolin, who has appeared in The Goonies, No Country For Old Men also comes back as Paul’s mentor and one of the last surviving members of his father’s court.

title: Philippa Gregory: ‘Some male historians don’t like women’s history’
body:
Nine years ago, the historian and best-selling novelist Philippa Gregory attended a funeral at Leicester Cathedral. It was an unusual service, not only because the deceased was royalty but because he had been dead for well over 500 years. The reinterment of Richard III, the last Plantagenet king whose remains were discovered in a car park in Leicester in 2012 was, says Gregory, “big and emotional. There was a beautiful hand-made pall over the coffin, which was preceded by two knights on horseback, one of whom had scoliosis, just like King Richard. Thousands of people lined the funeral route carrying white roses [the emblem of the House of York].”

As the coffin passed her in the Cathedral, Gregory recalls the church warden bowing and saying: “God bless and keep your Grace.” “That sense of time-slip was so inspiring for me,” she reflects. “As a historian in the modern world, you spend your time trying to imagine what life was like hundreds of years ago and, all of a sudden, you’re at the funeral of a medieval king.”

Gregory – who, at 70, has sold more than 10 million books, including The Other Boleyn Girl (made into a film in 2008 starring Natalie Portman and Scarlett Johansson), and The White Queen – is talking from her book-lined attic at home in Leicestershire. She is open and thoughtful, greeting questions with long pauses and choosing her words carefully. After the funeral, Gregory re-read Shakespeare’s Richard III, which famously depicts the monarch as a murderous villain and a “deformed, unfinish’d” hunchback (the bones found in Leicester revealed scoliosis of the spine, but no hunch). And so she dreamt up a project where she would re-evaluate Richard.

“I had already done a novel based on Richard III’s wife, Anne Neville, called The Kingmaker’s Daughter, where you get a different picture of him as a good king who was very concerned with modern concepts like social justice and freedom. But I wanted to write something that would focus on Richard and give a fairer account.”

That account is Richard, My Richard, Gregory’s debut play, which opens with its protagonist bursting from his grave in Leicester car park and learning, via the embodied figure of History, about the ways he has been maligned. Along with his alleged physical frailties, the drama also tackles the persistent narrative that he was behind the deaths of his nephews, Edward V and his younger brother Richard, known as the princes in the tower. While it’s clear the two boys disappeared, historians have found no evidence to show they were murdered; one theory is that they were smuggled out of the tower and to Europe. In any case, says Gregory, “there’s nothing that pins Richard to the crime”.

Though she has written Richard, My Richard in the iambic pentameter, she is not, she says, trying to rewrite Shakespeare. “I’d neither have the chutzpah nor the vulgarity to think that would be a good thing to do. But the Shakespearean view of Richard is, in a sense, evergreen, as the play continues to be shown. And I don’t think one should take Shakespeare’s account of history as [the true] account of history. The Tudor narrative” – in which King Richard is vanquished by Henry Tudor’s forces in the Battle of Bosworth Field – “absolutely depends on Richard being seen as a tyrant, and Shakespeare was a Tudor playwright.”

As well as being Gregory’s first play, Richard, My Richard stands out amid her body of work in focusing on a man. The author has made her name telling the stories of women pushed to history’s margins, or deemed significant only via their relationships to important men. Her most recent book, published last autumn, was Normal Women, a sweeping non-fiction account of the British women overlooked by historians, from factory workers and farmers to nuns and highwaywomen. It reveals how the Peasant’s Revolt of 1381 was sparked not by Wat Tyler, as schoolchildren have always been taught, but by two women from Kent, Joan Hampcok and Agnes Jekyn, who were protesting against a tax on married women.

“A lot of women have told me that the book made them feel very angry,” Gregory notes. “But having worked on it for so long, I saw that what is persistent is women’s success. You punish or ban women from one thing, and they just pop up somewhere else.” She adds that there’s never an advance in women’s progress “that isn’t immediately followed by a completely deliberate and sometimes legal attempt to put them back to where they came from. But just as the pushback is inexorable, so is the march forward. I’m a naturally optimistic person and when I look at the history of women, I feel optimistic and cheerful.”

When it comes to male pushback, Gregory has first-hand experience. She recalls how, in the 80s, when she began writing fiction, “historical fiction was a despised form of writing, because it was confused with historical romance. Basically, a historical period was just a vehicle to get your royal heroine into a low-cut dress. That was the point of it and anything else you learned along the way was just folderol.”

But rather than detailing the love lives of “pretty girls and handsome lords”, Gregory used the genre to examine serious themes around female history and the class struggle. Her first trilogy, Wideacre, tackled the injustice of primogeniture – where the son and heir, “no matter how useless”, gets the land – along with the politics of the village and the agricultural revolution.

“Of course, you’d never sell a historical novel telling people it’s about the agricultural revolution, so [the marketing] didn’t focus on that. But it didn’t necessarily endear me to some historians who like to see themselves as the guardians of the flame of historical accuracy and who don’t particularly like working people’s history or women’s history.” Among those loudly dismissive of her work was the Tudor historian David Starkey, who called it “good Mills & Boon”.

You wonder what Starkey would make of the fact that Gregory got an E in her history A-level, which she blames on the course being “just unspeakably dull. The topic was the wars of the Emperor Justinian in Europe. I really couldn’t stand it.”

After school, she trained as a journalist and did an apprenticeship at the Portsmouth Evening News. But, having realised she was spending more lunchtimes in the library reading fiction than in the pub with her colleagues, at 21 she decided to go to university and study English. Her course at Sussex University allowed her to do taster modules in other humanities subjects and, after spending two terms studying history, everything changed. “I thought, ‘This is what I’ve been looking for all my life. It explains why I am here, why these buildings are here, why this town is here. History answers everything.’ And I have worked, one way or another, in history ever since.”

When I ask Gregory whether there is such a thing as historical accuracy, there is another long pause. “Only in the sense of a dartboard,” she says eventually, “in that you can see where you want to get to, which is the red bit in the middle, but there is this spiral of accounts around it, and there’s the constant measurement of whether this account is more reliable than that one. So there’s a lot of processes you have to get through before you can say, ‘I know this happened on that day.’”

Richard, My Richard is an apt reflection of those processes. By allowing the monarch to grapple with the various beliefs about his life, it shows how history is essentially a series of rewrites and reassessments – a conversation with no end. “What I’ve tried to do with Richard is stay close to the historical record where it’s clear, and to be ambiguous about it when it’s ambiguous,” says Gregory. “For those who are on one side or the other [regarding Richard III’s villainy], that won’t be satisfactory. But this is history, and you can’t please everyone.”

‘Richard, My Richard’ is at Shakespeare North Playhouse, Prescot, 8-30 March, and Theatre Royal Bury St Edmunds 11-27 April shakespearenorthplayhouse.co.uk; www.theatreroyal.org
topics: Book Interviews, Books, Richard III, Theatre

title: How to lose the dad bod in 12 weeks (without spending 24/7 in the gym)
body:
So here we are, peak holiday booking season, beset by anxiety because it’s time to get rid of the dad bod, says Nick Harding

Not so long ago, the first signs of spring and the opportunity to ditch heavy coats and knitwear were a stress-free affair for men. No one cared if our winter-fed pot bellies poked out from under our T-shirts, we were forgiven because our physiques – softened by the passage of time, Hobnobs and beer – got a rebrand. We had dad bods.

Collectively brainwashed, we and our partners were lulled into believing that our bloated, pudgy torsos were the epitome of masculinity. We proudly exposed expanding midriffs and cloaks of matted body hair because women dug the dad bod.

Then came 2018, when the stage show Magic Mike opened in London and messed it up for all of us. So far almost half a million women in the UK have filed through its doors and emerged deprogrammed, the scales removed from their eyes by cavorting muscled hunks, all smooth, athletic, and glistening like porpoises.

They set a new standard for men to live up to. The dad bod didn’t stand a chance.

So here we are, peak holiday booking season, preparing for warmer weather, beaches and swimwear, beset by anxiety because it’s time to get rid of the dad bod no one wants anymore. It is a daunting task for a man at any time of life.

There is good news, however. While getting lean might seem Herculean , it doesn’t have to be. In fact there are three simple rules. Burn more calories than you consume. Don’t bother trying to target specific areas of fat, because you can’t spot-reduce fat. And nutrition is around 80 per cent of the battle, so you can’t outrun a bad diet.

Jack Claxton, expert personal trainer at David Lloyd Clubs, says we should start by going easy on ourselves.

“There’s nothing wrong with a dad bod, of course,” he counsels. “However, for those looking to change their physique, nutrition has to be number one. Without changing the balance of calories in versus calories out, it will be very difficult to reduce body fat, which essentially is how to reduce a dad bod.

“A couple of workouts a week from as little as 30 minutes can help build your fitness, stamina and muscle mass in the body.”

He recommends setting realistic, incremental goals to reach at four, eight and 12 weeks in order to keep your programme sustainable and consistent. These could include weight goals and active minutes per week.

Electric muscle stimulation, or EMS, is an ideal option for people who don’t have lots of time to spend in the gym. It uses electrical currents to activate muscle fibre while the participant is taken through a 20-minute exercise session. The results in a single session can be equivalent to, or better than, hours spent lifting weights in a gym.

Fraser Smith, personal trainer and founder of London’s EMS studio, Vive Fitness, says: “If you are time poor and want someone to keep you accountable for your exercise, EMS offers a focused, short, sharp all-over workout focusing on strength, flexibility and balance.”

Smith says that most people can find spare minutes in the day in which to add calorie-burning activity.

“Reprioritise what you do with your time. We can all find a few minutes during the day in which to fit some exercise. It is a question of motivation versus discipline. Reframe your perspective when you are not motivated to see it as a discipline. In five minutes, for example, you can do a squat, a lunge, a push/pull exercise, and a plank several times – you’ll feel a lot better for doing so. You may only have a few points in the day where you have a spare five minutes, but if you do some activity in this time, by the end of the week you’ll have added an extra hour of exercise.”

And Darren Newell, a Surrey-based personal trainer, explains how to optimise movements for maximum calorie burn.

He says: “Pack big compound movements into a workout to maximise the effort. So, if you are doing bicep curls with dumbbells, add a lunge. Or, if you are squatting with weights at your side, add a curl and then extend to a shoulder press. These big explosive compound movements engage much more muscle, which then uses more calories, giving you more effort in less time.”

Non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) is the calories expenditure achieved outside of exercise, eating and sleeping. NEAT activities are the ones we do without thinking. They include climbing stairs, walking, housework and even fidgeting.

Increasing NEAT increases calorie burn, as Newell explains: “If you are in an office job, for example, try to get up and move regularly. If you have a phone call, rather than take it sitting at your desk, get up and walk around. If the call lasts 20 mins, that’s a 20-minute walk. The cumulative effect of adding this type of activity, such as walking upstairs rather than taking the lift or escalator, will all help.”

Philip Chant, founder of body composition scanning company Bodyscan, adds: “An extra 8,000 to 10,000 steps might burn around 300 calories, which doesn’t sound much, but over a year that’s the equivalent of 14 kgs of fat.”

“There are a lot of calories in food but comparatively few calories burnt during exercise,” says Chant. “When you exercise regularly it consistently adds up. However, if the goal is to lose fat, 80 per cent of fat loss is about diet.” For this reason, any weight loss programme needs to concentrate on smart food choices.

Smith explains: “If you are committing to lose some weight while getting fitter, you will need a certain amount of discipline with what you eat. You don’t have to live like a monk, but you will have to make some trade-offs, especially if you have a busy schedule and frequently eat out or eat on the go. Get used to looking for the healthy options on the menu and be aware of what you’re eating.”

Healthy options could include swapping fries for salad, eating a starter and a side instead of a main, opting for steamed or baked options rather than fried, sticking to fish or chicken, instead of pork or beef, having sauces on the side so you can control the amount used and sharing a dessert or requesting a half portion.

Menus which list calories are useful, and often sobering. A pub Sunday lunch, for example, usually weighs in at a hefty 1,200 to 1,400 calories, even roast chicken. Add a dessert and that’s a whole day’s worth of calories in one meal. Then consider that there are more than 200 calories in a pint of beer and 125 calories in a glass of red wine and it becomes evident how easy it is to overeat when eating out.

Takeaways are also a minefield. Creamy curries and battered and fried Chinese are the worst offenders but sticking to Thai or lean meat kebabs – chicken or lamb – without chips are healthy options.

Intermittent fasting is not for everyone, but it can help as a method of calorie reduction, as can replacing a meal with a protein shake or product such as Huel.

Even seemingly healthy foods can have hidden calorific consequences, as Chant explains: “In Pret a Manger, for example, if you have a flat white, that’s around 100 calories, a chicken avocado and basil sandwich is 480 calories, and a cinnamon Danish is 410 calories. That’s close to 1,000 calories for an on-the-go lunch.

“An average man wanting to lose weight would be looking at a daily intake of around 1,900 to 2,000 calories a day, so that’s half your allowance already.”

He cautions to beware healthy foods. “Things like nuts, avocados and olive oil are all calorie dense,” he says. “If you are not using those calories they eventually get stored as fat, no matter how healthy they are.”

Other tricks and tips include clearing cupboards of temptations such as biscuits and crisps, and cooking with filling whole grain high fibre ingredients such as bulgur wheat, couscous, quinoa, beans and legumes such as lentils in place of white rice, pasta.
topics: Features, Gym, Health, Men, Weight Loss

title: I grew up in poverty post-WW2 – I feel like I’m ending my life how I started it
body:
One retiree with limited income opens up about how she makes it work

Yvonne Bailey, 79, vividly remembers what it was like to be raised in poverty in post-war England. For the family, living in Oxfordshire, food was very scarce, there was no heating and a constant nagging worry about money.

During the winter months, before school, her mum heated her clothes in the oven because they had become icy overnight.

For years, Yvonne fought to escape poverty. She moved to London at the age of 16 to find work. She worked long hours and saved every penny she could.

Then she met her former husband and together they raised a family. Some years, Yvonne said, they could even afford to go on holidays.

“Those years were the best years of my life,” she recalls.

But now, Yvonne said, she is counting money every day. After her husband died a decade ago, Yvonne moved out of their rental accommodation and into a social housing flat. She gave up her car. She learned how to budget and live within her new means – but none of this had ever been the plan.

“I simply didn’t think I’d end my life like I started it,” she says, referring to her life in late 40s and early 50s.

The worst thing, she says, is the feeling of jealousy. Growing up, even though several of her friends lived in social housing as well, it felt as if everything was harder for her family. She grew up without a father, so her mum needed to care for her and her siblings alone. She never had new clothes and was often hungry.

Now 79, Yvonne said, she often gets those same jolts of jealousy. Sometimes, she has to say no to a £4 coffee.

She is one of a fifth of pensioners in the UK who are living in relative poverty. This is the highest number since 2007/08, analysis of 2021 government figures by Independent Age show.

In total, 2.1 million retirees are living in severe hardship after paying their housing costs, with an additional 1.1 million living in financial insecurity just above the poverty line. People over 85 are most affected, and women worse affected than men, according to the charity.

Yvonne wishes she had spent more time learning about money when she was younger. She didn’t know then how much leaving time off work to care for children during her working years sunk her national insurance contribution, meaning that her state pension would have been higher. She also wishes she had learnt to pay her family’s bills so that she would not have found doing so such a shock after her husband died a decade ago.

Yvonne, who has spoken to i about why she believes the state pension needs to be higher previously, worked in hospitality for years. She thinks she has probably had more than 30 jobs since she started her first job at Thomas Cook in the 60s. She retired 20 years ago – and couldn’t wait for her last chapter of life to come after decades of hard work, including caring for two boys.

Now, she often feels lonely and anxious about money. She is close with her children, and has many good friends – some of which are several years younger than herself – and she is healthy. But life just isn’t the same as it was in her best years, she says.

There are some positives, Yvonne says, compared to when she was at her lowest. She has found a way to get pension credit and also inherited her husband’s state pension, after he died. Yvonne has no savings, but being a widow she entitled to housing benefit.

“It has taken away the concern of being able to afford that one cup of coffee or not,” she says.

Yvonne is active in the social scene, in Oxfordshire. She drinks coffee with her friends – sometimes they end up chatting for hours.

“My friends are an extended family to me,” she admits.

title: Why are mortgage rates still rising when the Bank of England base rate is not?
body:
Several lenders have increased their mortgage rates in the past few days - though experts predict this trend may reverse soon

Is the mortgage market turbulence getting you down? Have you got a mortgage-related question you need answering? Email in and we’ll get one of our experts to reply. Nick Mendes, mortgage technical manager at John Charcol, has given his advice to a reader below. If you have a question for our experts, email us at money@inews.co.uk.

Question: We’re coming up to remortgage in July and I am getting confused – why are mortgage rates seemingly continuing to rise when everyone says the Bank of England base rate is likely going to come down? I thought the two were linked?

Answer: Mortgage rates in the UK are shaped by various factors, and they differ among lenders. Each lender has its own approach to setting mortgage rates.

Understanding how fixed rates are determined is crucial. Lenders typically price their fixed rates against a swap rate also known as “SONIA Swap”. Swap rates are an agreement between two parties where they agree to exchange one stream of future interest payments for another. They are used by mortgage lenders to mitigate the risk in a fixed rate mortgage. One party agrees to receive a fixed-rate payment, while the other receives a variable payment.

Swap rates are influenced by market expectations regarding future interest rates. Presently, the market anticipates a gradual reduction in the rate over the next two years, tapering off after five years.

The Bank of England (BoE), like other central banks, changes the base interest rate as a primary tool to influence inflation levels in the economy. An increase in the base interest rate by the BoE makes borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses.

This, in turn, tends to reduce spending and borrowing, as individuals and companies become less inclined to take on new loans or financing. This decrease in spending helps cool down demand in the economy.

At the beginning of the year, the market was factoring in six to seven cuts to the base rate in 2024. Now, the expectation is for the base rate to be cut about three times this year, reaching around 4.5 per cent by December. This correction in early market predictions has resulted in an upward trend in mortgage rates since the start of February.

Markets are currently pricing in a base rate falling to around 3.8 per cent by the end of 2025, before eventually reaching 3.5 per cent in 2027.

It’s crucial to recognise that mortgage rates are influenced by a combination of factors. While the central bank’s policy rate is significant, it is not the sole determinant of mortgage pricing. Economic conditions, market dynamics, and lender-specific factors all contribute to the overall landscape of mortgage rate movements.

Whether you’re a first-time borrower or an existing mortgage holder, it’s strongly advised that you speak with a broker. A broker can compare rates in the ever-changing landscape across different lenders, ensuring you secure the most favourable terms up until the completion of your mortgage.
topics: Fixed-rate mortgage, Money Clinic, Mortgages, Remortgage

title: How I Manage My Money: PA, earning £900 a month, took £50k lump sum from pension
body:
Kat Vasili thinks the state pension is inadequate and is grateful she has a substantial workplace pension pot

In our How I Manage My Money series we aim to find out how people in the UK are spending, saving and investing money to meet their costs and achieve their goals.

This week we speak to Kat Vasili, 61, who lives in Hampshire with her daughter, Jane, 24. Kat’s other daughter, Lucy, 30, lives with her boyfriend. Kat worked for a large local authority in the social work sector for over two decades. She quit her job and took out a £50,000 lump sum from her pension last year and thinks the state pension is inadequate. Kat now works 16 hours a week as a personal assistant (PA) to five vulnerable older people.

My monthly income: Work pension, £1,560; rent from my daughter who lives with me, £100; income from my work as a personal assistant, around £900 a month.

My monthly outgoings: Mortgage, £500; groceries, £400; council tax, £175; gas and electric, £171; water, £36; petrol, £30; Sky broadband, TV and Netflix, £124; Spotify, £11; mobile phone, £53; car insurance, £28; TV licence, £13; health insurance, £40; Postcode Lottery, £12; Green Flag cover, £10; money into savings, £300. Any money left over is often spent on the garden, but we also have a takeaway once a month. I don’t own credit cards.

When it comes to money, I am risk averse. I grew up in the North East and we had to scrimp and save as a family.

I worked my way up to become a senior social work manager for a large local authority, earning around £67,000 a year. I worked in the sector for over two decades after getting a diploma and a degree in adult social care. I’ve always been passionate about care for the elderly and vulnerable.

However, the job became incredibly stressful and exhausting. By June 2022, I knew I needed to go. I was mentally exhausted and nearing 60. I wanted to retire early and do something which gave me more pleasure.

In August 2023, I quit my job for good. I took out a £50,000 lump sum from my defined benefit, or final salary, work pension. I could have taken out £100,000 tax-free, but decided to take out less so my annual income would be a bit bigger. I think my pension has over £400,000 in it in total. The salary sacrifice for years was worth it. As it’s an index-linked defined benefit pension, I’ll get a guaranteed annual income of around £20,200 a year before tax.

I’ll start claiming my state pension when I’m 67. I feel very fortunate that I’m not paying rent and have additional money coming in from a work pension. I don’t think the state pension is anywhere near enough to live on. It doesn’t equate to a living wage. Having seen the plight of many vulnerable elderly people, I do think there should be a conversation about whether the state pension could be means tested.

After leaving my job at the council, I worked out that I would need £600 to £900 a month on top of my pension to live on. So, in September 2023 I started working as a PA to five older people. I really enjoy it and do a whole host of jobs for them, including gardening, dog walking and ironing. Most importantly, I sit down and have a chat with them and keep them company.

I earn around £900 a month from my role as a PA, but this can vary. The income isn’t guaranteed and my clients’ circumstances can change. I’d much rather do this sort of work than get a job in a factory or supermarket.

I purchased my current home in 2010 for £215,000. It’s a three-bedroom semi-detached house with a lovely garden. I don’t know how much it’s worth now. I’m on a standard variable tariff offset mortgage, with £8,400 left to pay. The mortgage was taken out for a 15-year term and I have to get it paid off in full by September next year.

I am cautious when it comes to saving and prefer cash accounts. I don’t have any stocks and shares, but I do have a cash savings account which I add £300 a month to. I have about £3,500 saved up in it, but am looking to increase this.

I can manage well on the money I have coming in now. There’s a lot of debate about how much money people who retire need to live on. But I think I could easily live on £25,000 a year.

In terms of financial goals, my mortgage has to be paid off by September next year, but I’m hoping to get it all paid off in May. By the end of next year, I’d like the sum in my savings account to have reached £6,000. I’ll start putting £200 extra into the account each month. I’m not extravagant, but it’d be good to have an extra cushion available when needed. While I won’t be able to help my daughters get on the housing ladder, I’ll certainly help them with furnishing their properties when the time comes. I’m not keen on the idea of releasing equity from my home as it seems too risky.

At this point in my life, I’m more interested in what money can do for me rather than how much I’m making. I don’t have massive ambitions for my retirement and feel so grateful I have the flexibility to do the things I want now.

title: Nesting is hell dressed up as ‘protecting children’ – it made my divorce 100 times worse
body:
When nesting arrangements are abused, the house is no longer a place of safety, says one writer

My husband sends me a vicious text, complaining about the state of the shower. He’s been fishing the gloop out of the plughole, but leaving it in the middle of the shower tray for me to find when I return home. It’s not an oversight, forgotten as part of the bigger job of actually cleaning the shower. No. The matted black slop is left there to make a point. His message calls me “disgusting”. He mocks the fact I must be “nearly bald”. I’m “filthy”. “Lazy” too. This, from a man who never cleaned the shower once in the 20 years we were married. Now, apparently, it’s the hill he’s prepared to die upon.

This is my reality of living with a “nesting arrangement”, while we navigate an increasingly acrimonious divorce. My husband is right, in that my hair is falling out at an alarming rate. It comes away in ragged handfuls, as the stress of this supposedly constructive-parenting arrangement escalates. My home used to be a happy one. Now I dread coming back. My friends worry about how thin I am. I no longer sleep through the night.

Nesting means that the children continue to live in the family home, while parents take it in turns to move in and out weekly. Staying here together during the limbo of sorting out finances had quickly proved impossible for us. My husband morphed overnight into a frightening bully intent on making sure the children knew whose “fault” the wrecking of all our lives was. (Spoiler: mine, apparently). In desperation to prevent them witnessing any more conflict between us, and with a complicated financial situation preventing any obvious way to split our assets, I agreed to leave my home on a part-time basis to keep the peace.

What has happened since then is that I’m as trapped as I ever was. He drags out our divorce, refusing to sell the house. I can’t move fully out, or on. Meanwhile, he racks up debts in both of our names, and I’m powerless to stop him.

Perhaps naively, I’d imagined nesting could be the start of a new co-parenting dynamic. One where, unlike the past decade of my life, I wouldn’t have to carry the entire mental load of running our household. I’d imagined we might share jolly Sunday roasts at handovers, go for coffee together, continue the complex joint rhythm of ferrying our children to hobbies, just without the “we’re married” label attached. But joint parenting is so much more than just being where the children are. It’s the constant thinking ahead. The meal planning, the shopping, the endless logistics and planning around washing the PE kits in time. As the children’s primary caregiver, our nesting arrangement should have meant a step back for me and a step up for my husband.

What it shouldn’t have been was coming home after “his” weekend to find a filthy house where no-one has fed the pets for three days. The kitchen bin overflows. The sink is a greasy backwash of takeaways which must have passed as the children’s nutritious meals, the leftovers of which are still strewn all over the kitchen table. There’s no milk, no bread, no coffee, no washing done and no toilet roll. I have 15 minutes before I’m due to start working from home all day, which I now must spend driving to the shop to buy food for our starving cats. As I leave I notice he’s carefully lined up three empty champagne bottles on the counter above the bin. He is living his best life. I’m cleaning it up.

This isn’t a one-off. The carefully worded email I’d sent with some sensible principles for how we could considerately share our space as housemates instead of partners has been roundly and repeatedly ignored, and every time I come home the fridge is conspicuously empty.

Feeding the children on his days seems to mean buying just enough for one meal, and not a jot more – presumably lest I accidentally benefit in some small way too and enjoy a free biscuit I don’t deserve. He fights what he sees as the unfairness of me being here one day a week more than him with a thousand tiny acts of protest – financial and emotional. He has still never changed anyone’s bedsheets, washed the towels, cleaned the bathrooms or bought shampoo. I realised some months in that he was steadily removing joint items of value from the house while I was away too, leaving me unsettled and unnerved trying to work out what was different. It took photographing the wine rack to realise he was taking the expensive bottles one by one, rearranging what was left to disguise the absence over a period of weeks. What a guy.

Aside from the crashing absence of basic supplies and casual acts of malice, there’s something darker at play when nesting arrangements are abused like this. My home used to feel like a place of safety. Now, I surrender all my possessions twice a week to the care of a man intent on hurting me from a distance. If he hit me, there would be obvious consequences. But if he just…stops paying all the bills – what then? If we slide into arrears, what then? What if I pay everything I can towards bills in our joint names he used to cover in full, but it’s still not enough – what then?

I beg him to agree how we fairly split our outgoings, but he just ignores me. It’s inaction, weaponised. It’s not that he can’t pay. He just won’t. I’ve been lucky to find my first full-time job after years of child-rearing. I know I will need to support myself, but my husband is doing everything he can to teach me a lesson. That lesson is: how dare you try to leave. You will pay.

Legally, as both our names are on the bills, I’m still 100 per cent liable for the arrears he’s creating, even though I’m paying half. As the court summonses mount and my credit rating plummets, I call the utility companies once a month, begging someone to understand that this is financial abuse, to help me somehow. I dread these calls. I can’t make it through the explanation of what’s happening without choking on tears, a ball of panic rising in my throat as I feel the weight of payment processing systems stacked against me.

Patient call handlers explaining again that there’s nothing they can do as if he’s not paying then I must cover it all, while I shake and whisper I know, I know. I’ve been shown small kindnesses along the way – payment extensions, delaying the inevitable – but the systems just are not set up to separate the liabilities of divorcing couples where one party isn’t playing by the rules. And meanwhile, I bear the consequence. The debts rise. I do not sleep. My hair falls out.

For so many families, the rising cost of living has made normal life difficult financially, even on two incomes. For divorcing couples, it seems almost impossible to see how to turn one struggling household into two on half the income. Nesting can seem like a good idea in the face of this, a temporary stopgap to soften the blow of separation. But my advice to anyone thinking of doing it is this: hope for the best, sure. Aim to do divorce better, by all means. But just in case – plan for the worst.
topics: Divorce, Features, Marriage, Parenting

title: Solo female vanlife can be lonely – but this is why I’m desperate to go back
body:
Many 'vanlifers' find the lifestyle challenging, but the pitfalls can outweigh those of 'normal' life

I was 33 when I quit my 9–5 office job, bought a campervan and set out to explore life outside of the norm. What started as a summer adventure turned into almost five years on the road. There were challenges along the way, but for the most part, I had the time of my life. I loved the freedom and flexibility and that I was no longer stuck in an office. I found work as a marketing freelancer and writer, which provided me with flexibility and financial security. I met amazing people and explored New Zealand, my beautiful home.

I loved vanlife, and I’m not alone. According to the Office for National Statistics, in 2021, 104,000 households lived in caravans or other temporary structures in England and Wales, and Facebook groups like Vanlife – UK and VanLife UK have hundreds of thousands of members between them. Here in New Zealand, camping is hugely popular, with nearly a quarter of a million people freedom (wild) camping somewhere in the country annually.

However, after almost five years, I became increasingly aware of the downsides. The constant change, while exciting for many years, started to feel exhausting. My van still felt homely, but I dreamt of a permanent bed and full-sized shower. I still loved exploring new places but also longed for a sense of home and belonging.

Most of all, I missed being part of a community. As an introvert, I value close connection to a selected few. As a vanlifer, I met the most amazing people. However, forming deep relationships is hard when you’re constantly on the go.

Holly, a long-term vanlifer in North America, can relate. She shares: “I loved the freedom of vanlife. But I wanted to meet someone and start a family, which was hard to do on the road. So I returned to a more settled life.”

Like Holly, that longing for connection and community ultimately made me sell my van. I was drawn to the familiar, so I returned to Auckland, where I had lived before embarking on my vanlife journey.

The return to a more normal life proved challenging. Reconnecting with old friends turned out to be easier said than done since they had all chosen very different paths in life. I still loved them (and still do), but I didn’t feel as connected to them anymore as I once did.

Being back in Auckland also reminded me how much I dislike living in a big city and how expensive “normal” life is. The prospect of returning to a 9–5 office job just to keep a roof over my head and food on the table was depressing. It maybe didn’t help that I was working on a book about my journey at the time. It meant I still had one foot in that world and was acutely aware of the freedom and adventures I had given up.

For several months, I felt lost and unsure about what I wanted my future to look like. When an opportunity presented itself to housesit for three months in Nelson, an idyllic small town on the South Island, I took it as a sign to move there.

I left Auckland nine months after selling my van. I took a week off work for the move to Nelson, and it was then that I found myself again. Being back on the road – albeit with a car, rather than a campervan – reminded me how much I enjoyed vanlife. I started to miss it like crazy.

This sense of feeling torn between craving both freedom and stability is one many other nomads are familiar with. Helen Lockhart, originally from just outside of Portsmouth, has lived the nomadic life on and off for eight years with her husband and two boys. She can relate: “We paused our nomadic life a couple of times to be close to family. But the longing for adventure always makes us return sooner or later.”

Helen now works for adventure-focused PR agency Roam Generation through that has encountered many nomads who give the lifestyle up, only to miss it so much they return. It turns out I am not alone.

I didn’t settle in Nelson. Instead, I bought a caravan and returned to life on the road.

Vanlife isn’t perfect. But neither is “normal” life. Ultimately, I decided that, right now, I value freedom and time more than I value stability. I may now have found a way to have both.

I’m taking a different approach to vanlife this time around. I’m staying at one campground for a few months to create a base and community. After that, I intend to travel, but much slower, so I’m hoping it won’t feel as hectic. I will have my base to return to whenever I feel like it. Finally, the caravan is much larger than my previous van, so I now have that permanent bed and full-sized shower I used to dream of.
topics: Australasia Travel, Housing, Lifestyle, Motoring, Travel

title: Four things we get wrong about UPFs, according to a food science expert
body:
Saying that ultra-processed foods are like smoking is scaremongering and isn’t backed up by evidence, says expert

Last week saw the release of the latest study lambasting ultra-processed foods (UPFs) as the cause of our dietary ills.

The largest study of its kind, published in the British Medical Journal, found that UPFs are directly linked to 32 harmful effects to health, including higher risk of diabetes, heart disease, cancer and mental health issues.

Ultra-processed foods are foods that have been industrially refined using products not normally available in your home kitchen, such as emulsifiers, stabilisers and sweeteners, and make up over half of the UK’s daily diet. Amid concerns over their addictiveness and their impact on human health, there have been calls for them to be labelled and restricted in the same way as cigarettes. But how justified are our worries about UPFs, and how much do we really know?

Gunter Kuhnle, Professor of Nutrition and Food Science at the University of Reading, told i about five common myths about UPFs – that even the experts get wrong.

“The most common misinterpretation is that ultra-processed food and junk food are the same things. They are on entirely different scales: junk food is defined by composition and generally refers to foods high in fat, sugar and salt, while ultra-processed food is defined by the way it’s processed.

“Bread is an ultra-processed food in the UK, and I think most people would agree that bread is not junk food. Infant formula is an ultra-processed food but infant formula doesn’t really rate anywhere in these junk food scales.

“As a UPF is a question of processing not composition, the question then becomes when does something tip over into this category. I don’t see a problem with declaring Coco Pops ultra processed. But are fish fingers ultra processed or are they not? If I make a soup at home, cook it all from scratch, but then add a stock cube, is it then suddenly ultra processed or not?

“These things are very important, because if you really want to understand what is going on you need to have a clear definition. And without a clear definition the correlations and patterns are really, really difficult to take apart.

“What that means for people choosing what to eat is that they should really seek a varied, balanced diet and look at the entire dietary pattern, not individual foods. For example, are you eating a mix of fresh and prepared foods? How often do you rely on pre-packaged snacks high in fat, sugar and salt? It is also important to keep in mind that food is not just there to nourish but has many other roles.”

“It is very hard to actually know much about people’s dietary habits, even in detailed studies. If you tell me you’re eating a sandwich now, I have no way to know whether this is a homemade sandwich with bread you made yourself, cheese from a local farm shop and so on, or whether it’s a Tesco sandwich.

“Very often, questionnaires ask about what you eat based on a list of 140 foods, and by their very nature they have to be reductionist. So if they say ‘did you consume yoghurt’ we have no idea whether this is plain yoghurt or fruit yoghurt. So while it may be true on a population level to assume that bread eaten in the UK is ultra processed and bread eaten in France isn’t, that’s not going to be true on an individual level. But research relies on these broad assumptions.

“Based on the evidence we have, we can be fairly certain that fat, salt and sugar affect health – but data on ultra-processing are much weaker. While no policies are based on this data yet, there are currently discussions based on weak UPF evidence.”

“Does ultra-processed food cause poor health, or are unhealthy people just more likely to eat them? Many studies in this area are correlatory, not causal. We know, for example, that people who eat more UPFs are more likely to be poor, to smoke, to have a sedentary lifestyle and so on.

“So there are a lot of factors coming together and saying this causes that definitively is very difficult. Even in the most recent paper claiming UPFs have 32 harmful effects., the authors themselves rate most of the evidence as very low quality, simply because there are so many factors that can’t be addressed.

“If you actually read the study and look at the table where they grade the evidence, most of the 32 are rated as low or very low evidence. So if I were to interpret it I would not say there are 32 harmful effects. There are certainly some, especially obesity, type two diabetes and all cause mortality, but to claim there is this link is a strong statement that I wouldn’t make based on that data.”

“If we want to get people eating a healthier diet, we should choose the positive approach and talk about what to eat more of rather than saying ‘don’t eat processed foods’, going the other way around and saying eat a varied diet, eat more fresh things, eat more fruits and vegetables would be much easier and better for everyone.

“Saying that UPFs are like smoking is scaremongering and isn’t backed up by evidence. Smoking increases the risk of death much, much more than ultra-processed food. And you don’t have to smoke! There’s no need for you to smoke, but you do need to eat. It’s really pushing a scary narrative that is probably causing more harm than it helps.

“It also cements the wrong idea that ultra-processing is bad and therefore that processing is bad. Processing just means the food has gone through a transformative process – anything from fermenting (yoghurt) or baking (bread) to freezing (vegetables) or pasteurising (milk). These are all very healthy foods.

“In the end – and this might be very cynical – ultra-processed foods are not going to disappear. They’re durable, people like the taste, you can’t get rid of them. All you could do is try to make them healthier, and to do that you need to understand what actually makes them unhealthy.”
topics: Features, Health, Healthy Eating, Junk Food, Lifestyle

title: Andrew Tate arrives at Romanian court in handcuffs after arrest on UK warrant
body:
Lawyers for four women who accuse him of rape and sexual assault wrote to British police to request his detention over fears he would flee

Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan arrived at court in Romania in handcuffs on Tuesday morning, after European arrest warrants were issued by the UK.

Lawyers representing four women who accuse Andrew Tate of rape and sexual assault wrote to UK police to request his detention over fears he would flee Romania.

The social media influencer, 37, and his brother Tristan, 35, were detained after a European arrest warrant was issued by UK authorities for charges dating back to 2012-2015, the pair’s representative said.

They appeared before the Bucharest Court of Appeal today for a decision on whether the warrant should be executed.

The court postponed a decision on the warrant, and the men remain in custody.

A statement from law firm McCue Jury & Partners, the lawyers acting on behalf of Tate’s British accusers, said: “Last week, we received information that Tate might have been planning to flee Romania, where he is due to stand trial for separate allegations of rape and human trafficking.

“We wrote to the British police to bring this to their attention and to urge them to immediately seek a warrant for Tate’s detention in Romania and extradition to the UK.”

The law firm said Hertfordshire Constabulary is investigating allegations made by the four British accusers.

The Tate brothers are charged with rape, human trafficking and forming a criminal gang to sexually exploit women in a separate case in Romania, after being arrested in the country’s capital in December 2022 along with two Romanian women.

All four deny the allegations.

The Tates’ representative said in a statement today: “This bewildering revival of decade-old accusations has left the Tate brothers dismayed and deeply troubled.

“They categorically reject all charges and express profound disappointment that such serious allegations are being resurrected without substantial new evidence.

“The Tate brothers assert that the timing and circumstances surrounding the reappearance of these allegations raise serious questions about the motives behind this legal action.

“The suggestion that Mr Tate’s rise to fame may have played a role in these developments adds another layer of distress and concern.”

Commenting on the Tate brothers being detained, Matthew Jury, managing partner at McCue Jury & Partners, said: “Today’s news is very welcome as it has been a significant concern to many that Andrew Tate would seek to avoid justice in Romania and abroad.

“We are grateful to the British authorities for taking our concerns seriously and issuing an arrest warrant.

Mr Jury also called on the media not to give Mr Tate such wide exposure, saying: “Since his arrest in Romania, [Andrew] Tate has spread a vast amount of disinformation about the criminal allegations he faces in the UK in a series of high-profile interviews with individuals such as Piers Morgan and Tucker Carlson.

“We hope these recent developments will discourage them and others from continuing to give Tate such a platform or, at least, encourage them to properly interrogate him on the allegations.

“Allowing Tate to spread disinformation about the allegations of criminality he faces, not just in the UK, only helps to support and spread his toxic influence further amongst vulnerable younger men and boys, something we should all be seeking to put an end to.”

The ex-kickboxer’s representative said the pair “unequivocally deny all allegations”, and are “fully committed to challenging these accusations with unwavering determination and resolve”.

The statement added: “As the Bucharest Court of Appeal convenes today, the Tate brothers are still hopeful that the court will consider the broader implications of this case and its potential impact on justice and due process.

“They remain resolute in their pursuit of truth and justice, confident that the legal system will ultimately vindicate their innocence.”

Mr Tate has told his fans that the legal charges against him are a conspiracy to silence him.
topics: Andrew Tate, Courts, Hertfordshire, Police, Romania

title: Green anger as ministers promise new gas power plants ‘to avoid blackouts’
body:
Rishi Sunak says gas is needed to let UK hit net zero in a 'sustainable way that doesn’t leave people without energy on a cloudy, windless day'

The Government is to commit to building a new generation of gas power stations, saying it is needed to secure UK energy security.

Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho will outline the need for gas-fired power in the UK beyond 2030 to avoid the “genuine prospect of blackouts”.

Ministers insisted Britain would still meet targets to cut greenhouse emissions to zero overall by 2050.

Rishi Sunak said gas was needed so the UK could meet its emission-cutting goals in a “sustainable way that doesn’t leave people without energy on a cloudy, windless day”.

Gas would be needed to maintain UK energy security he said.

However climate change experts said the move showed the UK was “going backwards on energy security” after “fumbling” moves to boost wind power and energy efficiency.

Announcing the new gas strategy, Ms Coutinho is expected to say: “There are no two ways about it. Without gas backing up renewables, we face the genuine prospect of blackouts.

“Other countries in recent years have been so threatened by supply constraints that they have been forced back to coal.

“We will not let ourselves be put in that position, so, as we continue to move towards clean energy, we must be realistic.”

She will defend the move as the latest step to reach net zero in a “sustainable, pragmatic way that rids us of the need to rely on foreign dictators like Putin”.

The plans will include stricter rules for new plants to be built net-zero ready and able to convert to lower-carbon alternatives such as using hydrogen, or having carbon-capture technology to store emissions.

Ministers say the new plants would run less frequently as other low-carbon technologies, such as renewables and nuclear, are increasingly brought into operation.

The Government did not give any details about when or where the power stations would be built.

But Ed Miliband, shadow Energy Secretary, warned UK consumers would face “at least another 10 years of high energy bills and energy insecurity because of their plans.

“The reason the Tories cannot deliver the lower bills and energy security we need is that they are specialists in failure when it comes to our clean energy future: persisting with the ludicrous ban on onshore wind, bungling the offshore wind auctions, and failing on energy efficiency.”

Juliet Phillips, at climate change think tank E3G said: “The UK remains on track to be a clean power leader by 2030, having overseen continued exponential growth in renewables.

“However, due to policy failures over the last Parliament, the Government has missed opportunities to build out the full offshore-wind pipeline, to make gains in energy efficiency, or address clunky network connection times – all factors that mean new gas plants have been announced.

“These must come with strict conditions that new plants can be retrofitted with green hydrogen or CCS [carbon capture and storage] in the future, to maintain the UK’s clean power leadership.

“In addition, more political attention is needed to often overlooked power solutions – like long-term storage and demand side flexibility – in order to get the UK off volatile fossil gas imports for good.”

Jess Ralston, at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit said: “The Secretary of State suggesting that if we cannot control energy prices then we are not secure as a country, while announcing new gas power stations, has a real irony about it.

“Anyone paying an energy bill in the past two years knows that the UK doesn’t control the price we pay for gas, that international markets decide.

“The UK is going backwards on energy security because of the Government fumbling its latest auction for British offshore wind farms, failing on its home insulation schemes and dithering on heat pumps.”

Liberal Democrat energy and climate change spokesperson Wera Hobhouse MP said that announcement was “another step backwards on the critical road to net zero.

“We need to wean ourselves off this reliance on expensive fossil fuels by investing in cheap, clean renewable power and insulating every home.”

Meanwhile, energy regulator Ofgem has called for suggestions on how to help protect consumers amid high energy costs, and find ways to reduce a record £3.1bn pile of unpaid bills.

“Many people have been struggling to pay their energy bills and this risks becoming an enduring problem,” said Ofgem’s Tim Jarvis.

Ofgem has previously said the UK should consider launching a social tariff for household energy which would see those most vulnerable and least able to pay charged a lower price for their power, but added that that is a decision for ministers.

In January, i reported that plans to launch a social energy tariff for vulnerable households had been quietly shelved by the Government.

The promise to consider a lower energy tariff for certain consumers were first made in 2022 and reiterated by Rishi Sunak last year.

But sources indicated it was no longer a priority – with ministers looking at other ways to help those in need.

Ministers previously said the Department for Energy and Net Zero would launch a public consultation in summer 2023 – but it has not been forthcoming.

A Government spokesperson said it was supporting vulnerable households through additional payments and would keep “all options under review”.
topics: Claire Coutinho, Climate Change, Climate Crisis, Energy, Gas, Net zero

title: More people out of work as unemployment rate rises and wage growth slows
body:
First rise in jobless count since July, and more than a fifth of adults are not looking or not available for work, figures suggest

Wages have slowed as unemployment rose for the first time since last July, latest figures show.

The unemployment rate went up to 3.9 per cent in the three months to January from 3.8 per cent in the previous three months, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

Vacancies continued to fall while redundancies rose, in clear signs the UK economy was starting to respond to the high interest rates.

Average regular pay growth, excluding bonuses, fell to 6.1 per cent in the period, down from 6.2 per cent in the three months to December and the slowest growth for more than a year.

More than a fifth of adults in the UK are economically inactive – not actively looking for work in the final months of 2023 – official figures suggest.

The UK’s economic inactivity rate was 21.8 per cent between November and January, higher than a year earlier.

Liz McKeown, of the ONS, said: “Recent trends in the jobs market are continuing, with earnings, in cash terms, growing more slowly than recently but, thanks to lower inflation, real-terms pay continues to increase.

“The number of job vacancies has also been falling for coming up to two years, though the total remains more than 100,000 above its pre-pandemic level.

“Over the last year, there was little change in the proportions of people who are employed, unemployed or neither working nor looking for work, though the overall number of people in work is still rising.”

The Chancellor, Jeremy Hunt, said: “Our plan is working. Even with inflation falling, real wages have risen for the seventh month in a row. And take-home pay is set for another boost thanks to our cuts to national insurance which in total are putting over £900 a year back into the average earner’s pocket.”

Paula Bejarano Carbo, an economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “ONS figures indicate the annual growth rate in average weekly earnings, including bonuses, was 5.6 per cent in the three months to January, and 6.1 per cent excluding bonuses.

“While these figures remain high by historical standards, allowing households to regain some of the purchasing power lost during the post-Covid period of high inflation, wage growth continues to soften.

“We expect wage growth to return to historical levels as the labour market continues to loosen, potentially prompting the Bank of England to consider cutting interest rates in the near future.”

Tony Wilson, of the Institute for Employment Studies, said: “The jobs figures show that the labour market remains pretty subdued.

“The employment rate is broadly flat but still about one percentage point below where it was before the pandemic, even though unemployment has fallen back to where it was.

“There are fewer people in work because there are more people outside the labour force altogether – not looking or not available for work. In all, there are well over half a million more people out of work than before the pandemic began.

“This is being driven by more young people and older people outside the labour force, and in particular because of more people reporting long-term health conditions that stop them from working.

“In our view, this is holding back the recovery as the economy is continuing to create jobs, with nearly a million unfilled vacancies reported today.

“This reiterates that we need a different approach to how we reach and engage with people who are out of work and may want to come back to work, and in particular our employment services need to be more accessible, inclusive and supportive.

“Employers need to play their part too, and do more to keep people in work and to open up opportunities for those who may need more support.”
topics: Economy, Jobs, Pay, Unemployment, Wages, Work

title: Eric Carmen, Hungry Eyes and All By Myself singer, dies aged 74
body:
The Raspberries frontman 'passed away in his sleep over the weekend,' his wife confirmed

US singer Eric Carmen, who was best known for hits Hungry Eyes and All By Myself, has died in his sleep aged 74, his wife has confirmed.

The Ohio-born star rose to fame as frontman of the Raspberries before establishing himself as a solo artist with hit tracks including Hungry Eyes, which featured in the 1987 film Dirty Dancing.

Other major hits include 1975’s All By Myself, which features in the classic opening scene of Bridget Jones’s Diary, and was later covered by Celine Dion.

He wrote Almost Paradise, featured on the Footloose soundtrack, as well as Never Gonna Fall In Love Again and Make Me Lose Control.

“It is with tremendous sadness that we share the heartbreaking news of the passing of Eric Carmen,” a statement from his wife Amy said on the singer’s official website.

“Our sweet, loving and talented Eric passed away in his sleep, over the weekend.

“It brought him great joy to know, that for decades, his music touched so many and will be his lasting legacy.”

She ended the statement with the quote “love is all that matters… faithful and forever” from his 1977 solo album Boats Against The Current.

Carmen co-founded the Raspberries in the early 1970s alongside Jim Bonfanti and Wally Bryson, who were later joined by Dave Smalley after the departure of John Aleksic.

They released their debut album Raspberries in 1972. Their track Go All The Way was later banned by the BBC in the UK for sexually suggestive lyrics and was included on the 2014 Guardians Of The Galaxy soundtrack.

After four albums together, the band broke up in 1975 and Carmen embarked on a solo career.
topics: Music, US

title: i morning briefing: Why is the Government redefining extremism?
body:
The move is highly contentious and comes as many tensions are already running high

Welcome to Tuesday’s Early Edition from i.

This week Michael Gove is expected to unveil a new official definition of extremism, in a move that has already stirred widespread and high-profile controversy. In 2011 the counter-terror Prevent strategy defined the term as “vocal or active opposition to fundamental British values, including democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and mutual respect and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs.” Now that is being updated, as part of Rishi Sunak’s drive to crack down on Islamist extremists and far-right groups. The new definition is expected to include anyone who “undermines” the country’s institutions and its values. We’ll take a look at what the Government is planning to do, and what it could mean, after the headlines.

Rishi Sunak is under pressure to return money from the Tories’ biggest donor after a report claimed he said looking at Diane Abbott makes you want to ‘hate all Black women’. The Guardian reported that Frank Hester also allegedly called his “foreign” workers together to defend himself against claims of racism, adding: “We take the piss out of the fact that all our Chinese girls sit together in Asian corner.”

Right-wing Tory factions have blamed Rishi Sunak’s leadership for the defection of Lee Anderson to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party and demanded an “urgent” change of course from the Prime Minister. The former Conservative deputy chairman was unveiled as Reform’s new MP at a surprise press conference on Monday morning.

Kensington Palace ‘should have done more to protect Kate’ over photo blunder. A royal historian said it was “totally inept of Palace aides and communicators to have allowed this to happen on their watch,” reports Cahal Milmo.

The Government cannot afford to increase spending on defence, a minister has admitted, despite fears that the UK could be dragged into a war with Russia. More Conservative MPs added to a growing feeling of dissent over the failure of Jeremy Hunt to increase funds in the Budget, after two ministers broke cover to demand an immediate increase in spending to 2.5 per cent of GDP.

Drivers in south east England are set to face lengthy delays this weekend due to the “unprecedented” closure of a five-mile stretch of the M25. The UK’s busiest motorway will shut in both directions between junctions 10 and 11, in Surrey, from Friday night until Monday morning. See all the closures on our map.

A British doctor helped a woman give birth while 35,000ft in the air on a passenger jet. Junior doctor Hassan Khan delivered a healthy baby girl after a fellow passenger went into labour while on a flight from Jordan to London over the weekend.

How is the definition changing? The one set out under Prevent was previously accused by human rights groups Liberty as being so broad that “thousands of people are being swept up by it – including children engaging in innocuous conduct, people protesting climate change, and a nurse who began wearing a hijab.” It continued: “In fact, more than nine out of ten Prevent referrals in 2017/18 didn’t require any de-radicalisation action.” The new definition won’t just change the wording, it will also ban individuals and groups who “undermine the UK’s system of liberal democracy” from public life. It was reported last year that the definition of extremism would be the promotion of any ideology which aims to “overturn or undermine the UK’s democracy, its institutions and values; or threaten the rights of individuals or create a permissive environment for radicalisation, hate crime and terrorism”. It would also include: “sustained support for, or continued uncritical association with organisations or individuals who are exhibiting extremist behaviours.” According to the Observer, the new definition changes from “active opposition” of British values to identifying extremism “through behaviours that enable the spread of extremist ideology”. However the Communities Secretary is not expected to publish a list of extreme groups caught under the new definition, despite calls from campaigners and Conservatives to name and shame organisations.

What would it do? Under the proposals being considered, expected to be revealed towards the end of this week, the new definition of extremism would ban anyone in Whitehall, Government bodies or quangos from engaging with or funding groups or individuals thought to be linked to extremism in some way. The rule would be non-statutory, so would only affect the organisations and individuals that receive funding or engage with Government bodies, officials and ministers. There will be no new criminal offences.It would be likely to mean that organisations and individuals which breach the new definition will be excluded from meetings or any engagement with ministers, senior civil servants, Government advisory boards, and funding. Read more here.

What are the concerns? There are fears that the broad terms would sweep up too many groups, have a chilling effect on free speech, inflame already existing tensions, and lead to legal challenges. Yesterday a dozen high profile figures signed a letter warning about the risk of politicising anti-extremism, voicing concerns about freedom of speech. Among the signatories were three Tory former home secretaries – Dame Priti Patel, Sir Sajid Javid and Amber Rudd. They warned a change to the legal definition could have sweeping implications for free speech and urged both main parties not to politicise the issue “to seek short-term tactical advantage” in the run-up to the general election. A wide range of campaigners have also warned against the move, from LGBT campaigners to former anti-apartheid activists. Even the Countryside Alliance has spoken out against it. Tim Bonner, the chief executive, told the Guardian: “We are concerned that defining extremism as something as woolly as ‘undermining fundamental British values’ will become an excuse to crack down on any opinion which isn’t shared by a majority of the population. Real British values fundamentally respect minority views and do not seek to silence them,” he said. There are also fears about naming groups. i understands that as well as concerns about legal challenge, Mr Gove has been warned by officials that doing so could put people belonging to those groups in danger. Read that story here.

European countries must rebuild their defences further and faster as they face an increasingly antagonistic Russia and a potential Donald Trump presidency that is drawing the US from Nato, according to a top EU policymaker. Influential Belgian MEP Philippe Lamberts said that while most European countries are covered by Nato’s security umbrella, they should not take the guarantees for granted.

Elusive Melania ‘living separately from Trump’ but could still be a secret weapon. The former US first lady’s public outings over the past six months can be counted on the fingers of one hand.

A former Boeing employee known for raising concerns about the firm’s production standards has been found dead in the US. John Barnett had worked for Boeing for 32 years, until his retirement in 2017.

Scientists have identified the world’s first-ever cases of bird flu in king penguins, amid signs that the virus is spreading through the sub-Antarctic region. A team including British experts confirmed the H5N1 strain of avian influenza in five king penguins on the southern coast of South Georgia.

US singer Eric Carmen, who was best known for hits Hungry Eyes and All By Myself, has died in his sleep aged 74, his wife has confirmed. “It is with tremendous sadness that we share the heartbreaking news of the passing of Eric Carmen,” a statement from his wife Amy said on the singer’s official website.

Scientists are ‘baffled’ by a new species of strange organism found in a deep sea dive near New Zealand. More than 100 other marine animals were also discovered in one of the remotest parts of the ocean.

Ghislaine Maxwell, who is set to appear in a New York court to appeal against her sex trafficking conviction.

Lee Anderson gives Prime Minister a Reform headache. It is obviously unhelpful for Rishi Sunak that Lee Anderson defected to Reform UK, says Hugo Gye.

You’re wrong about ADHD, Matthew Parris. Come and meet my kids to learn the truth. Debating whether the condition can be misdiagnosed is one thing. Denying its very existence is patently absurd, writes Jessie Hewitson.

The Princess of Wales has only fuelled the furnace of conspiracy. There are calls for the original photo to be released — which might be wise, advises Jennie Bond.

‘Some male historians don’t like women’s history’. Philippa Gregory on the snobbery around historical fiction, the challenge of accurately portraying the past, and how her first play, ‘Richard, My Richard’, gives a fresh account of Richard III.

Four things we get wrong about UPFs, according to a food science expert. Saying that ultra-processed foods are like smoking is scaremongering and isn’t backed up by evidence.

The football coach who told his kids he got sacked – then posted video online. Former Cardiff manager Mark Hudson tells i about what he’s learnt as he continues to look for a job.

How to lose the dad bod in 12 weeks (without spending 24/7 in the gym). So here we are, peak holiday booking season, beset by anxiety because it’s time to get rid of the dad bod, says Nick Harding.

The Prime Minister’s spokesperson has said that alleged comments made by Frank Hester about Diane Abbott were “clearly unacceptable,” but refused to say if they were racist.

On Monday, The Guardian reported that Mr Hester, who has donated £10m to the Tories in the past year, said looking at Ms Abbott makes you want to “hate all Black women” and that she “should be shot”.

Ms Abbott said that the alleged comments made about her are “worrying” and have left her feeling “frightened” and “vulnerable”.
