title: The M25 closures mapped as chaos set to hit football fans and major airport routes
body:
Drivers are being urged to ignore satnavs and only follow official diversion routes to avoid causing gridlock

Drivers in south east England are set to face lengthy delays this weekend due to the “unprecedented” closure of a five-mile stretch of the M25.

The UK’s busiest motorway will shut in both directions between junctions 10 and 11, in Surrey, from Friday night until Monday morning.

Drivers have been asked to avoid the area if possible during the closure, which will be the first scheduled daytime all-lanes shutdown on the M25 since it opened in 1986.

National Highways said the action is necessary to enable a bridge to be demolished and a new gantry installed.

The government-owned company has urged motorists to ignore satnavs and only follow official diversion routes to avoid causing gridlock.

Here’s everything you need to know:

The M25 will shut in both directions between junctions 10 and 11 from 9pm on Friday 15 to 6am on Monday 18 March.

The five-mile stretch passes through Surrey, on the outskirts of Greater London.

National Highways, which operates and maintains the UK’s motorways, has warned that drivers across the region should expect lengthy delays, urging them to only travel if “absolutely necessary”.

It estimates that drivers who follow signs for diversion routes on A-roads will have an hour added to their usual journey times between junctions 10 and 11.

But the company is concerned that some may try to find alternative routes via minor roads.

National Highways project lead Jonathan Wade said how well the area copes with the M25 closure will partly depend on whether drivers ignore satnavs and stick to official diversions.

He said: “How many people are going to take the initiative and try and use satnavs?

“There’s probably a greater risk of congestion by people just doing their own thing and thinking they can perhaps beat the signs and find a shorter or quicker route.

“That will cause further congestion on some of the key junctions so please avoid doing that if at all possible.”

National Highways senior project manager Daniel Kittredge said: “If people move away from diversion routes that we prescribe, it creates additional issues in different parts of the road network.

“The majority of the time that will be local roads, so that really impacts residents in those particular areas.

“That’s why we’re trying to encourage people to not follow the satnav.

“Stick on the prescribed diversion route. It’s going to be more suitable for your journey.”

According to National Highways, the following diversion routes will be in place:

The M25 normally carries between 4,000 and 6,000 vehicles in each direction per hour from 10am until 9pm at weekends between junctions 9 and 11.

The closure is expected to impact more than 200,000 journeys, including many in and out of London.

Journeys to and from Heathrow and Gatwick airports will also be affected, along with motorists heading for Channel crossings in Kent.

Modelling carried out while the plans were being developed estimated that drivers would face delays of up to five hours without mitigation measures, such as discouraging travel and creating diversion routes.

National Highways believes only around an hour will be added to journeys because of the steps it has taken, which is based on a reduction in traffic of 50 per cent.

But Mr Wade said: “Because it’s so unprecedented, we’ve got nothing to benchmark it against.”

He added: “There’s never been a closure of this nature. We really can’t be certain how many people will heed the messages which we’ve given.

“It’s very difficult to determine right now how effective all our traffic management will be.”

RAC spokesperson Alice Simpson warned that drivers could face a month of “double traffic trouble”, with delays also expected over the Easter weekend due to additional travel.

She said: “With the M25 closures and the Easter getaway both falling in March, it could be a month of double traffic trouble for drivers trying to get around London or access Gatwick and Heathrow.

“Despite fair warning, the reality is most holidaymakers seeking to use either airport will have booked their trips months ago and will have to leave a lot more time to get there – not least because the most obvious diversion routes are likely to get extremely congested.

“Whenever delays are anticipated around bank holidays, it’s always best to set off as early as possible and avoid travelling during peak hours like late morning and lunchtime.

“As the M25 is notoriously one of the busiest routes in the country any increase in drivers could lead to more breakdowns, and even more jams.”

A spokesperson for Gatwick advised drivers to check diversion routes before they travel and allow for extra time.

“Gatwick’s train station is well connected and is a great an alternative option for people travelling to the airport this weekend”, they added.

Direct trains run to Gatwick from London Blackfriars, City Thameslink, Farringdon, London St Pancras and London Bridge. The Gatwick Express also runs from London Victoria, taking just 30 minutes.

You can reach Heathrow via the Elizabeth line, which also runs from Farringdon, taking around 90 minutes. The Piccadilly line goes to terminals two, three, four and five.

Another option is the Heathrow Express, running from London Paddington.

At least 30 major live events will be affected over the 57-hour period. They are:

Friday 15 March

Saturday 16 March

Sunday 17 March

National Highways said the action is necessary to enable a bridge to be demolished and a new gantry to be installed.

The five-mile closure is part of a wider £317m project by National Highways.

Due to be completed in summer 2025, it will increase the number of lanes and make it easier to enter and exit the M25 at junction 10 – one of the UK’s busiest and most dangerous motorway junctions.

Four more daytime closures of the motorway will take place up to September.

title: Lee Anderson gives Prime Minister a Reform headache
body:
It is obviously unhelpful for Rishi Sunak that Lee Anderson defected to Reform UK

Reform UK has risen without trace. A party with low name recognition and not much of a core message has slowly, quietly attracted the support of one in eight voters – and now it has its first MP too.

It is obviously unhelpful for Rishi Sunak that Lee Anderson defected to Reform on Monday. Just a couple of months ago, he was the Conservatives’ deputy chairman, and he is one of the higher-profile Tory backbenchers thanks to his outspoken media interventions and weekly show on GB News.

Let’s not get carried away. Mr Anderson had already been suspended by the Conservatives over a rant about Sadiq Khan, and his background as a Labour activist suggests a grasp of loyalty which is weak even by the standards of MPs. So there is little reason to think many colleagues will follow him to the Reform fold.

Previous Eurosceptic parties could attract support around the issue of Brexit; now there is no comparable rallying cry that unites disillusioned right-leaning voters who are fed up with the Conservatives.

So there are reasons to doubt how far the party can really rise, and indeed whether it can stop the bulk of its voters fleeing – however reluctantly – back to the Tories once the sharp end of an election campaign approaches.

That does not relieve the Prime Minister of a headache, at least in the short run. While some Conservative MPs have rallied round, others have accused Mr Sunak of driving Mr Anderson away; and, more importantly, driving away the voters who sympathise with Reform’s new representative.

We return, yet again, to the central point of British politics right now: Labour is on course for a huge electoral landslide, the Tories for a humiliating defeat. Opportunities for a reset at No 10 are running out.
topics: Lee Anderson, Politics, Reform UK

title: UK weather: Flood warnings as heavy rain to batter Britain
body:
Alerts issued across England, Scotland and Wales, with some residents advised to take immediate action

Flood warnings have been issued for parts of the England, Scotland and Wales, with heavy rain forecast to spread across Britain this week.

As of Tuesday afternoon, 50 Environment Agency flood warnings, where flooding is expected, and 147 flood alerts, where flooding is possible, were in place.

The majority are in south-west England, including coastal areas of Cornwall, Devon and Dorset.

In some areas residents have been warned to stay away from beaches, promenades and coastal footpaths and take immediate action to protect themselves.

Motorists are advised to plan driving routes and avoid low-lying roads near rivers. Householders are being urged to activate any property flood protection products, such as flood barriers and air-brick covers.

Fog, any frost and early bright spells in the east, will give way to a generally wet and breezy morning tomorrow, as outbreaks of rain feed across the UK from the west🌧️🌬️ pic.twitter.com/LgDJmOELLH— Met Office (@metoffice)

Flood warnings and alerts have also been issued by the Scottish Environment Protection Agency and Natural Resources Wales.

The highest ground in the west will see the heaviest rain, with up to 30-40mm forecast over the hills and mountains of north Wales, the Met Office said.

Strong winds, reaching around 30-40mph, will accompany the downpours.

The Met Office said heavy rain will gradually clear to the east leaving a drier and cloudy afternoon on Tuesday, although light outbreaks of rain will still be possible.

Met Office meteorologist Alex Burkill said: “Although temperatures are going to be higher than on Monday, highs around 13 or 14C, it won’t feel particularly pleasant, especially in those blustery winds and in any heavier rain.”

On Tuesday evening, outbreaks of light rain will become heavier and more persistent across Northern Ireland and Scotland.

The rain is set to continue throughout the week, but there will be some fine and dry weather in the south-east at times before it turns milder.

Temperatures are expected to reach the low to mid-teens in parts of the north later this week, and upper teens in a few southern areas.

title: Boeing whistleblower John Barnett found dead
body:
Former employee had previously made allegations about production defects and safety problems

A former Boeing employee who had raised concerns over potential safety problems and had been giving evidence in a whistleblower case against the company has been found dead, according to authorities.

John Barnett, 62, died from a “self-inflicted” wound on 9 March, the Charleston County coroner in South Carolina confirmed.

Mr Barnett had worked for the plane manufacturer for 32 years, until 2017, and made a series of allegations about the firm in 2019.

He told the BBC that workers under pressure had deliberately fitted planes with sub-standard parts and that passengers on its 787 Dreamliner could be left without oxygen in the event of a sudden decompression.

He said he was concerned a push to get new aircraft built meant safety was compromised, the BBC reported.

The company denied his claims.

Mr Barnett had also filed a whistleblower claim against Boeing alleging the company retaliated against him for reporting problems. He had recently been giving evidence in the claim.

In a statement, Boeing said: “We are saddened by Mr Barnett’s passing, and our thoughts are with his family and friends.”

The office of Charleston County Coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said: “Charleston City Police Department is the investigating agency. No further details are available at this time”.

Boeing has faced scrutiny over its safety record since two fatal crashes involving the Boeing 737 Max in 2018 and 2019.

In January this year, it came under renewed pressure after an unused cabin door on one of its 737s was blown off at 16,000 ft.

On Monday concerns were raised again when at least 50 people were injured after a 787-9 Dreamliner “froze” in mid-air after suffering a fault while flying from Sydney to Auckland.

Passengers reported “screaming” as the Latam Airlines Dreamliner went into a “nosedive” on Monday, with people thrown up in the air.

New Zealand’s Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC) said on Tuesday that it was examining the plane’s cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.

The accident investigator said Chilean authorities had confirmed they had opened a probe into the flight, and it was assisting with their enquiries. The flight, LA800, was ultimately bound for Santiago in Chile.

A TAIC spokesperson said that because the incident on the Sydney-Auckland flight occurred in international airspace, it fell to Chilean accident investigation authority Direccion General de Aeronautica Civil (DGAC) to open an inquiry.

The cause of the apparent sudden change in trajectory of the flight is currently unexplained. Safety experts say most airplane accidents are caused by a cocktail of factors.
topics: Air Travel, Aviation, Boeing, Planes, Safety, USA

title: Europe must prepare for twin threat of Russia war and Trump presidency
body:
The British Army is ‘overextended’ and should take action immediately, says senior MEP Philippe Lamberts

BRUSSELS – European countries must rebuild their defences further and faster as they face an increasingly antagonistic Russia and a potential Donald Trump presidency that is drawing the US from Nato, according to a top European Union policymaker.

Influential Belgian MEP Philippe Lamberts said that while most European countries – including Britain – are covered by Nato’s security umbrella, they should not take the guarantees for granted, given Mr Trump’s antipathy towards the alliance.

“If Russia were to take on Nato now, we would be a match,” he told i. “But that doesn’t mean that we should be complacent, because the Russian army is more battle hardened than it was at the beginning of the campaign. And this cannot be said of all the European armies.”

Mr Lamberts, co-leader of the European Parliament’s Green alliance, noted that while all Nato countries were boosting their defence budgets, the real challenge for Europe’s militaries is the duplication of defences.

“The first thing that we need to do is to get more bang for its buck,” he said. “In the EU, we have spending in 27 different ways, we have 27 national defence apparatuses so the money is not going into stockpiles. We are not where we need to be.

“And we are too dependent on others – and if you can’t count on the Americans, then you’re left with domestic capabilities. And we are, again, not where we need to be.”

While Britain is, along with France, the biggest European military power in Nato, Mr Lamberts, the former co-chair of the Parliament’s Brexit Steering Group, said it was also lagging.

“Even though it has one of the biggest armies in Europe, it’s still overextended. Its strength has never been the British Army but rather the Royal Navy and the Royal Air Force. And you can see that they are they are stretched thin. In recent manoeuvres, the UK has two new aircraft carriers … but they are plagued by problems,” he said.

Last week, the European Commission unveiled plans for a European Defence Industry Strategy, to pioneer initiatives such as strategic stockpiling, with officials saying the bloc is facing a “security paradigm” with an expansionist Russia operating a wartime economy as it presses into year three of the conflict with Kyiv.

Announcing the initiative, EU internal market commissioner Thierry Breton said: “To counter the return of high-intensity war on our border, we have decided to kick up a gear.

However, raising budgets is not enough, according to Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council in Washington DC.

“Nato is about the defence of the territory of its members, which it has been practising for 75 years. But where we are not ready for a conflict with Russia, is in the non-military domain,” she said, adding there was little preparedness for conflict in the “grey zone” of hybrid warfare such as cyberattacks, disinformation or infrastructure attacks.

“The reason it’s so difficult in the grey zone is that it’s extremely hard to predict what the other side will do. And then when it happens, it’s totally unclear how we can respond or retaliate if, say, the other side engages in massive cyber-aggression, or blows up infrastructure,” she said.

Ms Braw added that European countries, including the UK, needed to be more candid about the risks.

“We need to be much more open and transparent with the public about the threats. Because if our governments, with the best of intentions, don’t tell the public about it, then the public will assume that things are fine.”
topics: Donald Trump, Europe, Nato, Russia, Vladimir Putin

title: Russian military cargo plane crashes after catching fire with 15 on board
body:
The Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft crashed north-east of Moscow after one of its engines caught fire, the Russian defence ministry said

A Russian military cargo plane crashed shortly after take-off in the country’s western Ivanovo region, the defence ministry in Moscow has said.

The Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft crashed at about 1pm Moscow time on Tuesday after one of its engines caught fire, the Russian Tass news agency reported, citing the country’s ministry of defence.

There were eight crew members and seven passengers on board at the time of the crash north-east of the Russian capital, the ministry said. It did not say if there were any survivors, but the governor of the Ivanovo region, Stanislav Voskresensky, expressed condolences to the families of “the deceased pilots of the Il-76 crew”.

An anonymous emergency service official told Tass: “According to preliminary data, everyone on board died.” The source added that a search was underway for flight recorders.

A photo posted on the Ivanovo region government channel on Telegram showed Mr Voskresensky at the scene of the crash.

“The fire at the scene has been extinguished. No populated areas were damaged,” he said.

The plane was heading to the Severny airfield near the city of Ivanovo when it crashed in a forest near the village of Podtalitsy, about six miles from the air base, according to the Russian independent news website Meduza.

A witness told Tass that the plane crashed near Bogorodskoye cemetery, east of Severny, saying: “It fell and exploded.”

Unverified videos on social media appeared to show a plane with one engine on fire as it descended towards the ground.

In January, a Il-76 military transport plane crashed in the Belgorod region near the Ukrainian border. Russia blamed Ukraine for shooting down the plane, and claimed all those on board, including 64 Ukrainian prisoners of war, were killed. Ukraine did not confirm or deny Kyiv’s involvement in the plane crash.

The Il-76 aircraft is designed to carry troops, cargo, military equipment and weapons, and has been in service in the Soviet and Russian air force since the 1970s.
topics: Russia, Russia-Ukraine war

title: I’m not sharing my bed with boyfriends anymore
body:
Picture the scene: its 2am in the morning and I am lying in bed, wide awake. The man beside me is sleeping like a baby, and why wouldn’t he be? He has the podcast he “needs” to fall sleep playing loudly beside the bed. The room is suffocatingly warm because he “just can’t sleep with the window open”, and sleep he most certainly has, because he is now snoring like a water buffalo.

I try to roll him over to stop the noise, which I succeed in doing, but he takes the duvet with him. I spend the remainder of the night burying my head into the pillows to block out Joe Rogan ranting about bears, only to throw them off again when my head starts to overheat. I don’t get a wink of sleep. Around 7am he stirs and reaches for an embrace.

“Isn’t it nice to sleep together?” he asks.

No! No, it sodding well isn’t, and I am tired of pretending it is! It’s awful. Why on earth have we made sleeping together in the same bed a measure of a healthy relationship? It’s madness. Unless we are viewing it as some kind of endurance test to prove you can put up with a partner’s night sweats, that simply makes no sense to me. Two people were unconscious in the same place at the same time. Big deal. I had the same experience in a field with a security guard I met at a music festival in 2005 – that doesn’t mean I was in love with him.

Don’t get me wrong, I understand the fantasy of sleeping together, and I see the appeal. After a long, weary day, two sleepy rabbits snuggle into one another, beneath the crisp, fresh sheets, and slowly drift off, holding one another close in a warm embrace until they awake, refreshed and more in love than ever. There are probably bluebirds singing on the windowsill and woodland creatures serving breakfast. But seriously. Who actually sleeps like this? At best, you have managed to acclimatise to one another, like prison cellmates, but isn’t it time we just admitted that we all sleep better on our own?

My optimal sleep conditions require total darkness, absolute silence, a nest like configuration of pillows that I have arranged to support my hips and back, and the window open a crack. Yes, I am one of those people. I don’t care if it’s below freezing outside, the window will be open. (I’m a 42-year-old woman, for goodness’s sake. I overheat at night.) I want space when I sleep, and I want my own mattress, which is firm to the point of rigid. I want my pre-pre-alarm to go off at 5am to get me ready for my 6am pre-alarm, before my actual alarm goes off at 7.00. And I want the radio on, tuned to the station I like.

You should also know that, even if I didn’t want all of the above, I am a nightmare to sleep with. All my life, I have had a terrible problem with sleepwalking and night terrors. My mum has installed cowbells on the doorknob of the spare room so she can hear if I’ve wandered off in the middle of the night when I’m staying with her. I snore. I grind my teeth. I thrash about. I am about as far from the fantasy of the sleeping bunnies as you can get. Picture trying to spoon that kid from The Exorcist, and you’re somewhere close. This causes me so much anxiety, that even when a partner is prepared to meet my exacting sleep conditions, I still struggle to fall asleep with them because I’m terrified Night Kate will emerge and make a break for it.

You may have read that and shuddered at the thought of having a sleepover at mine, but isn’t that the point? Everyone’s sleeping habits are different and they are not always compatible. In my own room, I have created my ideal state of sleeping homeostasis, but it doesn’t take much to throw it out of whack. I bet you’re the same. In fact, if you are in a long-term relationship and you share a bed, I bet you have both had to make compromises on your preferred sleeping conditions, but why should you? Why can’t we just have separate beds, in separate rooms? I know that’s a privilege a lot of people simply don’t have, but why isn’t sleeping apart the ideal living arrangement instead of a marker of a failing romance?

Now, I will concede that there is some research that shows when you are in synch with your partner, sleeping together can bring some health benefits. I should point out the same benefits have been found for those co-sleeping with a pet, but let’s stick with the humans for now. One paper from the University of Arizona found that co-sleeping can reduce stress and anxiety, as well as improving the overall quality of sleep, but – and this is a big but – only if the couple actually managed to sleep soundly. For those of you out there dealing with snorers, flailers, walkers, talkers, and the lunatics who won’t open the damn window, it is a very different picture indeed.

Research from the Sleep Foundation found that “75 per cent of respondents who share a bed with a snorer say the snoring impacts their sleep and 77 per cent say it affects their well-being in some way”, and that “44 per cent of those who sleep with snorers say their partner’s snoring makes them tired the next day, 33 per cent say they feel cranky or moody, and 28 per cent have no energy”. How many of us are staggering through the day, cranky and moody, because we don’t want to admit that sharing a bed sucks?

One 2007 paper, published in Sleep Medicine Reviews, found that “a substantial body of evidence suggests that marital status is associated with sleep outcomes, with the divorced typically having more sleep problems compared to their married or single counter-parts”. And is it any wonder? If I had to sleep with me, I’d divorce me too.

Do you have any idea how bad a lack of sleep is for you? I can understand sacrificing your sleep for a newborn – they really can’t help what they are doing – but why do it for a grown adult who refuses to believe they snore? The cumulative effects of sleep deprivation have been linked to hypertension, diabetes, obesity, depression, heart attack, stroke, and premature morbidity (that’s dying early, in case you were wondering how serious this is).

You really don’t have to lose that much sleep for there to be a significant impact on your health. In fact, regularly sleeping for less than five hours a night has now been shown to significantly increase the risk of depression. And even if you manage to escape heart attacks, stroke, depression, and dying young, why should anyone have to spend the next day in a sleep deprived daze when they could just go and sleep in another room? Why do we keep doing this to ourselves?

The answer to that seems to be because we associate sleeping apart with a struggling relationship, rather than the state of bliss it actually is. According to the Sleep Foundation, 56 per cent of those sleeping with a snorer “never or rarely sleep in a separate room due to the snoring. Of those, 38 per cent say they don’t because they don’t want to sleep apart”. Are we really that attached to the fantasy of sleeping together that we are willing to endanger our health to do it? It certainly looks that way.

I’ve never slept well with someone else in the bed, and yet I have spent years of my life doing just that, because I thought that’s what you’re supposed to do. It’s nice to sleep together, right? Well, it isn’t if you don’t get any sleep, and I know I am not on my own here.

I suspect that a lot of this is just not wanting to voice how uncomfortable you find a partner’s sleeping habits. It’s not easy to speak up and break the fantasy of slumbering together in a bower of bliss. This is particularly difficult for women to do. Did you know that men sleep better with a partner than women do? Meanwhile, sleeping with a man has been shown to actually reduce sleep quality in women. If I had to take a guess at why that would be, I would say it’s because women struggle more to voice their own needs. They are far more likely to say its fine for a partner to play whale noises all night long if that’s what he needs to go to sleep rather than to tell him to pack it in.

I think we need to change this script. If you are sleeping sweetly with your partner, fabulous (though you may want to check they feel the same because you could be the problem). But if you are like me and struggle to sleep with someone else in the bed, then we need to start speaking up.

Being sleep deprived is not romantic. It is not a sign of a healthy relationship if you dread going to bed with someone because you know you are going to be kept awake.

Let’s normalise sleeping apart from one another. Let’s allow our loved ones the space they need to snore, fart, and babble in peace.

Having an entire bed to yourself? Now that is my idea of romance.

title: Two modest Budget policies that will have radical consequences
body:
“Headroom” has become a surefire winner in games of Budget Bingo – the word is always going to be uttered by the chancellor of the day.

It refers to the capacity the Chancellor has between what he wants to do and the amount of money he has available, and ever since George Osborne created the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), chancellors must defer to its calculation.

The OBR functions as a rabbits-out-of-hats regulator, restricting any surprise announcement the Exchequer might deploy to ambush the opposition or delight the electorate. It’s why so much Budget speculation is not about the Government’s political strategy, or the Chancellor’s cunning plan, but what headroom will be allowed by the almighty calculator-wielders.

Given that constraint, and very real economic limitations, Jeremy Hunt was told he simply couldn’t afford much beyond his National Insurance change. So he had to narrow his search to a more niche form of policy – more modest steps, with limited cost, but with the potential to produce a disproportionate positive impact.

These are rare, because a lot of low-hanging fruit has already been gobbled up, and they are not exciting – superficially, at least – because the glam, showy stuff has already attracted attention.

The ideal policy is limited in scale and involves technical tinkering, but is well-targeted to deliver bang for buck. It won’t set pulses racing, but it should improve the bottom line, where it really counts. You might call the criteria “dull clout” – practical, effective, but unsexy.

Now the dust has settled, there are two wins in Hunt’s speech that fall into this category. Each has an economic benefit, and together they tell a political story about the next couple of years.

The first is the lifting of the High-Income Child Benefit Charge threshold from £50,000 to £60,000 and the extension of the accompanying taper. (See, I promised technical and unsexy, and I have immediately delivered.)

This means you start to lose your Child Benefit once you earn £60k, instead of £50k. And the rate at which you lose it is more gradual, ending the benefit once your earnings reach £80k, compared to £60k before. The immediate impact is more parents will have more money in their pockets – a welcome boost to the electorally crucial, financially squeezed “Newly-Not-Young”.

Even better, this policy lowers an obstacle to both earnings and tax revenues. The old £50k threshold and the rapid taper produced a sky-high effective marginal tax rate. Tax Policy Associates calculated this at a staggering 71 per cent – a parent earning £49,999 lost 71p for every £1 of any extra income they received.

That is a concrete deterrent to work – the very thing the Treasury says it wants to incentivise. People turn down pay rises, shun overtime, and cancel startups and sidehustles because this rate makes it not worthwhile to earn more – a distortion which hobbles the economy and limits the tax take.

So this dull change has real clout. It doesn’t eliminate the elevated marginal rates (Hunt also promised to investigate switching the threshold to household income, which would be fairer than individual salaries) but it makes it a bump rather than a wall, reducing the peak from 71 per cent to 57 per cent. It’ll be interesting to watch salary and earnings in that £50k-£80k bracket to see how much income growth is unleashed.

The second such measure is the reduction in Capital Gains Tax for residential property from 28 per cent to 24 per cent.

Technical? Yes. Unglamorous? No doubt. Impactful? I reckon so.

This is the product of a rare consensus between the Treasury and the OBR that this tax cut will generate more revenue. As the Chancellor joked, “Perhaps for the first time in history both…have discovered their inner Laffer Curve.” (You had to be there. And be a fiscal policy geek. Trust me.)

More money is always music to the Treasury’s ears, but this is even better: more money from profits crystallised by the sale of residential property means it’s likely more properties will be sold as a result. In other words, they can raise more tax by releasing more housing into the supply-constrained market.

Two policies, neither of which will set the world ablaze but each of which holds the prospect of genuine, concrete benefits nonetheless.

Economic reality places a growing premium on ideas which offer this dull clout, and policymakers on all sides of politics are in search of more. Watch out for action on the massive marginal rate that hits parents at £99,999 of income, for example, which produces a major distortion in work for a higher earning cohort.

There’s a political lesson here, too: optics can be the enemy of practical improvements. Each of these ideas is tricky to sell to voters, because they lack glitz, while each is easy to attack with cheap rhetoric. Communicating their benefits takes more time than deriding them as “tax cuts for the better off” or “tax breaks for landlords”.

If you campaign in poetry but govern in prose, this poses a challenge to the Labour Party. The temptation to deploy such lines must be huge. But before long, they may be in power, themselves searching for just such prosaic policies with the dull clout necessary to ungum the economy and boost the public coffers. So don’t dismiss unsexy, technical but beneficial ideas – to a Chancellor without much headroom, they’re priceless.
topics: Budget, child benefit, Jeremy Hunt, Subscribers

title: The Chelsea and Newcastle stars who impressed Gareth Southgate – and who flopped
body:
Southgate took a watching brief at Stamford Bridge as he prepares to name his final squad before Euro 2024 this week

On Thursday, Gareth Southgate names his final England squad before Euro 2024 ahead of this month’s friendlies against Brazil and Belgium.

There is little time to make finishing touches to a side that, rightly or wrongly, will go into this summer’s tournament as co-favourites alongside France.

With just 23 making it onto the plane, the Three Lions boss spent Monday night in west London taking in Chelsea’s 3-2 victory over Newcastle United and casting an eye over six England hopefuls – with varying degrees of success.

PALMER – PASS

It was an unfortunate exchange with Tim Sherwood in his post-match interview – “all you need is some players to play with”, quipped the former Tottenham Hotspur and Aston Villa boss.

But Sherwood was right, of course, and the fact Cole Palmer has been a rose amongst so many thorns at Chelsea makes it virtually inconceivable that he will not make it to the Euros. The 21-year-old delivered another goal and assist to take his tally to 19 league goal involvements this season.

STERLING – FAIL

Palmer might have had another too, had Raheem Sterling squared it rather than holding on too long before attempting to shoot. Sterling also failed to even get one of his best opportunities on target.

The real question is how much that will actually shape Southgate’s thinking, as the forward has not made one of his squads since the Qatar World Cup in 2022.

Unless there is a chance of manager, it looks increasingly possible that his international career could be over at 29, however much Southgate intimates that the door will always be open.

GORDON – FAIL

On the one hand, Anthony Gordon was unfortunate to suffer a knee injury before he had the chance to impress – but Southgate had probably already seen enough.

There is no doubt about his attacking capabilities – 10 goals and five assists in all competitions – but question marks will be raised against his positioning.

Had Gordon not given Malo Gusto free rein down the right, Nicolas Jackson’s opener inside six minutes would not have happened (Sven Botman was an even guiltier party for clearing Gusto’s cross to Palmer, who delivered the assist). Gordon was having such difficulties with Gusto that he switched wings before going off.

LIVRAMENTO – PASS

Newcastle’s man of the match against his former club. Replacing the injured Kieran Trippier at club level and could soon do the same for the national side.

He is still eligible to play for Scotland and Portugal (through his mother and father respectively) but he has come up through the age groups with England and all the indications are that is where his senior allegiances will lie.

BURN – FAIL

Given England’s dearth of options at left-back, Burn has been mooted as an outside prospect but hardly boosted his chances here. Failed to block Gusto’s shot for the opener and struggled with Palmer all night, albeit he did not have enough protection in front of him until Miguel Almiron stepped in.

Who Southgate turns to instead is unclear. Luke Shaw is out for months with a leg injury, Ben Chilwell was absent again on Monday night and England could head into the Euros having to rely on Rico Lewis, Fikayo Tomori, or ask Trippier to switch flanks.

GALLAGHER – PASS

Set up Mykhailo Mudryk’s brilliant finish and looked energetic as ever, despite missing three days of training last week with a virus. Chelsea’s dire financial fair play situation means Gallagher faces a summer of uncertainty but there can be little ambiguity over his England place.

title: The football coach who told his kids he got sacked – then posted video online
body:
Former Cardiff manager Mark Hudson tells i about what he's learnt during his time away from football as he continues to look for a job

Last year, a video of Mark Hudson went viral. It was never the intention of him or his wife Marie-Louise, who posted it to Instagram, but that’s how these things tend to happen. The short clip spliced together the reaction of two of their three children, Ollie and Leo, as they heard the news first that their dad had got the job as Cardiff City assistant manager and then had lost his job as the club’s manager 14 months later. Go and watch it; it’s simple and it’s beautiful.

Another 14 months on, Hudson is looking for work again after a spell coaching at Sheffield United ended when Paul Heckingbottom lost his job as manager. He has recently spent time with both Ipswich Town and Norwich City on separate trips, gaining insight into how different roles operate in clubs he has never worked at and watching multiple training sessions. As he explains, this is as much a psychological endeavour as a practical one.

“Those trips are incredibly valuable when you are between jobs, because they challenge you,” Hudson tells i. “Sometimes you may have things that you thought were good practice confirmed by someone else, but there’s also always something new to pick up. That might be a coaching drill, or a specific way that a manager works with an individual player.

“I’m pretty hard on myself and don’t really give myself praise – I didn’t really do that as a player either. So if you go into clubs and listen to conversations, it can confirm certain things you’ve done. It becomes the praise that you haven’t given yourself, even subconsciously.”

That question of praise is an uncomfortable one for Hudson and others because football presents an inherent psychological problem. Self-improvement is an obsession for those within it, as Hudson describes through his own consumption live and via the sofa. But it’s also a pursuit in which no degree of obsession can ever lead to perfection.

So what does that do? Further fuel the obsession.

You constantly strive to better yourself. You constantly doubt that you are doing enough. You watch and you look for tactical developments and patterns that seem to shift every six months because you are afraid of getting left behind and then what’s going to happen.

For ex-players, the problem is surely worse because they have already been through it all once before.

“Even when I finished playing, I never felt like I had completed anything,” Hudson says.

“I had completed a journey, in terms of the time and the impact upon my body, but in terms of what you could possibly achieve or be better at, I wasn’t close. So it becomes all-consuming.

“It’s a 24/7 job, in and out of work. When I was manager of Cardiff, I look back now and cannot remember when there was a waking minute when something didn’t need my attention.

“The phone is always on. You’re drifting off to sleep and you’re thinking about the next morning: what scenarios might pop up, which players need something from you tomorrow.

“It’s its own planet – everything revolves around it. It takes all of your energy, but then it should, because you want to do everything to be successful. This isn’t sacrifice; it’s choice.”

A post shared by ML Hudson (@keepme4ever_thehudsonlife)

Choice that has to have an effect on those around you. The video of Hudson and his children gained fame not because it was an innocent and heartwarming moment captured and shared, but because it was something new. We have precious little appreciation of how football’s relentless cycle, its blame game, its short-termism and its instant switch to the next guy, affects the support network around its actors. What we saw was a glimpse into a world that we – even those of us who share the obsession – had barely considered.

“Here’s an example: my wife and I talk quite a lot about forever homes,” Hudson says.

“We’re in a house now that we have renovated to make it perfect for us, but it will be the third time that we have done that. They don’t want to move, I get that. The schools are good, friends and family are great and local. There are clubs for the kids. We love where we live.

“But there’s a lack of permanence to everything. The constant state is not change itself, but waiting for change.

“Someone once said to me that it’s like the army, where you can be shipped off somewhere new with little notice. Nothing is forever, and football breeds that short-termism. You have to learn to enjoy the good moments when they come along, and accept the emotional baggage.”

Two things get you through it: the love for the sport and the love of that family. The love of the sport makes you push yourself, put yourself out there by visiting clubs and having daily conversations that might go nowhere or somewhere and moving to Cardiff by yourself for a while if you have to because you don’t want the kids to move school again. The love from your family makes it all worth it because it’s them you’re doing it all for anyway. You are submerged in a team sport environment and you, together, are a team too.

“My kids ask me every day ‘Have you got a job yet?’ or ‘What are we doing next?’” Hudson says.

“That ‘we’ is so important because that shows their investment in it, even as children, but it comes with pressure. My eldest is 13 and is obsessed with football – playing, watching, reading about. Most mornings he will sit at breakfast and ask me ‘Anything going on?’, which is quite funny.

“Hopefully something comes up soon, but it has to be the right situation. I’m looking forward to whatever that is, but I can say this confidently: you’ll get all of our time and all of our excitement and our will to do well. The kids will be wearing the shirts on matchday. It’s that support that makes the whole thing easier for me and the whole thing worth it too. You will get all of me and all of us.”
topics: Cardiff City FC, Championship, Sports Interview

title: The three players who have transformed Arsenal
body:
Invincible member Martin Keown says there are three regular first-teamers who have made all the difference to Arsenal's title challenge

For one brief moment, you might have mistaken Arsenal’s win over Brentford for a Genesis gig, when Collins and Gabriel came together in the box.

Instead of Phil and Peter though it was Nathan Collins and Gabriel Magalhaes, centre-halves of physical stature matching the musical reputation of their namesakes.

The confrontation was anything but collaborative or musical, though Gabriel was quickly joined by his footballing front man William Saliba. Collins was quickly shouted down as the Premier League’s best defensive pairing showed they were prepared to back each other up on and off the ball.

Since first playing together on Saliba’s Arsenal debut in 2022, they have shared the pitch 53 times in the league, averaging a staggering 2.38 points per game. That trumps anything their title rivals can mount.

So what is the secret to a great centre-half partnership?

“Time, experience, dealing with certain situations, getting caught out, making mistakes, learning from them, coming back stronger, bouncing back,” says Martin Keown, who will be on TNT Sports duty on Tuesday night for Arsenal’s Champions League clash with Porto, where they will try to overturn a 1-0 deficit.

“They’ll be very proud of that clean sheets record.

“If you’re a defender in an Arsenal team, you don’t really get much credit because it’s all about the goals that are scored. In my day it was the same thing so we thought like we need to… If we concede, we’re gonna get criticism because they will say we’re the weak link in his team, and we made sure we weren’t.

“They’ll be doing the same building that reputation and they are. They’re strong. These two central defenders are really strong, quick.”

But it is not only about them. Keown formed a legendary partnership with Tony Adams in the 90s, conceding just 17 goals in the entire 1998-99 league season, a record that seems entirely unbreakable.

And this version of the Gunners, as defensively sound as they are, will not threaten the Premier League clean sheets record of 25 either, set by Chelsea in 2005, even if they do not concede another goal all season. Arsenal lead the league with 11 but that mark set by Jose Mourinho’s side looks likely to stand the test of time. Football, people say, has changed.

But the value of a defensive midfielder who can both defend and attack remains the same.

“Declan Rice is really going to another level right now,” Keown says

“I was very much spoilt with Patrick Vieira and Emmanuel Petit fighting for man of the match every week, [then later] Gilberto Silva and Ray Parlour. I’m not going to complain about what I had!

“His development has been huge because at the start he was looking like a central defender playing in midfield: he doesn’t look like that any more.

“His finish the other day, that was a really difficult half-volley finish. He’s expecting to get assists and expecting to get goals.

“At West Ham, he was covering massive distances and a really important figurehead at the back but now he does both for Arsenal.”

Keown is not the only one to have noticed, with manager Mikel Arteta taking time to single out Rice after Arsenal’s eighth league win in a row on Saturday, a late 2-1 victory over Brentford in which the England midfielder scored his sixth goal of the season.

“He’s playing at a very consistent and excellent level in different positions, in a new club,” Arteta said.

“There’s a lot of things that have to go together and it’s not easy, he’s done it with such determination, with the passion and quality that he knows he plays the game and understands the game, and he’s delivering some big moments for us.”

What Rice, Gabriel and Saliba all share is their integral role in Arsenal’s league-leading set piece machine. A mid-season trip to Dubai, since which Arteta’s men are unbeaten domestically, was where Rice proved himself to staff as a corner-taker, and the two defenders have six goals between them, all from corners, directly or indirectly.

With the title race arguably close than ever before, those strikes have been invaluable to Arsenal’s challenge.

“I think they could do something big in Europe, Arsenal this season,” Keown adds.

“They’re in that sort of tunnel now that you need to get into where you eat, breathe, sleep, football. And it looks like they’re on to wait on their way to doing something special.”
topics: Arsenal FC, Premier League, Sports Interview

title: Why Lewis Hamilton’s first F1 title is being challenged in the High Court
body:
Felipe Massa feels he was robbed of the 2008 world championship by the 'Crashgate' scandal in Singapore - and now wants justice

Felipe Massa wants what he believes should be his: the 2008 F1 world title.

He has filed a lawsuit in London against the FIA, Formula One’s ruling body; Formula One Management, who ran the sport at the time; and Bernie Ecclestone, who was the commercial rights holder, in order to try and achieve that.

Essentially, he is challenging what he claims is the combined failure of the regulatory body and the sport’s owners to cancel the results of the inaugural Singapore Grand Prix, in which Nelson Piquet Jnr deliberately crashed his Renault to aid team-mate Fernando Alonso’s prospects of winning, which Alonso duly did.

Massa eventually lost out in the championship race by a point to Lewis Hamilton in a dramatic finale.

When Massa took the chequered flag in the final race of the 2008 season, in his home country of Brazil, he sincerely believed he was the champion, not realising until he was rounding the Curva do Sol on his slowdown lap that Hamilton had passed Timo Glock’s Toyota in the final corners to claim fifth place and the points he needed to take his first world crown.

Massa was devastated, but magnanimous in defeat.

The truth of what happened in Singapore did not emerge until Piquet left the team the following year and told how team principal Flavio Briatore and engineer Pat Symonds had staged the whole thing.

In September 2009 the FIA charged Renault with conspiracy and race-fixing and ordered the guilty parties to appear before the World Motor Sport Council.

Renault had intended to fight the claims before accepting the charges, informing the FIA that Briatore and Symonds had left the team.

Briatore was banned for life and Symonds for five years, later reduced on appeal, but the FIA allowed the race result to stand.

That appeared to be that, until Ecclestone revealed in an interview given to F1 Insider last year that the details of the crash were in fact known to the authorities in 2008, and not as previously stated at the point of Piquet Jnr’s revelation in August 2009.

“Max Mosley and I were informed during the 2008 season what had happened in the race in Singapore,” Ecclestone was quoted as saying.

“Piquet Jnr had told his father Nelson that he had been asked by the team to drive into the wall at a certain point in order to trigger a safety car phase and such to help his teammate Alonso.

“Piquet Jnr was worried about his contract extension, so he was under a lot of pressure and agreed. We decided not to do anything for now.

“We wanted to protect the sport and save it from a huge scandal. That’s why I used angelic tongues to persuade my former driver Nelson Piquet to keep calm for the time being.”

Ecclestone subsequently distanced himself from the version of events as presented by F1 Insider, claiming he didn’t remember the interview, but that did not stop Massa pursuing what he sees as justice.

Theoretically the drivers were affected equally by being forced to respond to the incident.

Massa, along with most of the drivers in the race, came into the pits behind the safety car after Piquet engineered his crash on lap 15.

Though Massa was leading at the time of the incident on the 15th lap, he left the Ferrari pit box with the fuel hose still attached and had to stop at the end of the pit lane to allow the mechanics to remove it.

He was later hit with a penalty for an unsafe release and finished outside the points. Hamilton finished third to claim six points.

Massa argues that had the incident been investigated when the truth was discovered by the authorities in 2008, and the results annulled, he would have won the championship by five points. That’s the maths of the matter.

Massa’s lawyers have asked for all documentation relating to the race and the subsequent FIA investigation to be made available, claiming their client was the “victim of a conspiracy” with the authorities seeking to avoid a scandal.

Papers were filed at the High Court in London on Monday. Massa insists he is fighting for justice and the integrity of the sport.

As a rule, courts tend to take a dim view of participants stepping outside of a sport’s own regulatory framework to settle cases.

Even if the truth of Ecclestone’s anecdotal timeline is established, it would have still required retrospective action.

And it doesn’t alter the fact that the FIA considered the case, albeit the following year, and elected not to change the outcome. It is their sport, their rules.

A court ruling in favour of Massa would open a panoply of retrospective cases seeking to right sporting wrongs.

You can imagine Hamilton being the first to file papers with regard to the events in Abu Dhabi in 2021, where he lost the world title to Max Verstappen following a safety car incident that did not conform to FIA regulations.

England would, perhaps, seek redress for Diego Maradona’s illegal Hand of God goal that knocked them out of the 1986 football World Cup.

Similarly West Germany, who lost out to England in 1966 to a goal by Geoff Hurst that VAR would have ruled out today, could lay claim to a fifth World Cup.
topics: Courts, Lewis Hamilton, Singapore, Sports Explainer

title: A Very Private School review: Charles Spencer’s brave and gruesome abuse memoir
body:
The earl's grim revelations about the paedophilic sadism and abuse he suffered at boarding school is impossible to read without feeling fury and disgust

Earl Spencer’s grim revelations that he was groomed by a school matron at the age of 11, and subjected to the paedophilic sadism of the headmaster John Porch, have grabbed headlines ahead of the publication of this book.

What a heartbreaking read it it is. Charles Spencer, historian and brother of Princess Diana, provides a stark account of his time at the Northamptonshire boarding school Maidwell Hall in the 1970s and the emotional, physical and sexual abuse he suffered there due to a culture of bullying and secrecy.

It is brave for such a high-profile aristocrat to come forward with pull-no-punches candour: Spencer can draw attention to shameful practices that have long been covered up or diminished. Yet there have been harrumphing articles implying that such tough schooling was merely character-forming. This book is surely a resounding rebuttal of that view: it would be hard to actually read it cover to cover and not feel disgust, and fury, on behalf of the children put through such a system.

This is not a one-man crusade: alongside his own calm but vivid first-person account, the earl presents testimony from many fellow pupils. The Maidwell scars are long lasting – several former pupils speak of how their time there decimated their confidence or sense of joy, or prevented them from being able to love as adults. Several also report that their buttocks still show signs of caning, four or five decades on.

Reading the gruesome details, all this is hardly surprising. Porch would be visibly aroused while caning boys, and would grope his favourites while beating them. Another teacher hit one child so hard he fell unconscious, and forced another boy to swim for so long he almost drowned. The same teacher forced a pupil to use his naked body and erect penis as a “human slide” when entering the pool.

Earl Spencer partly coped by turning on himself: he would make himself sick, considered shooting himself in the foot. When the abusive matron told him she was leaving Maidwell, he cut himself with a penknife. While that may sound surprising, the earl is admirably honest about the complexities of his feelings for this 20-year-old woman who kissed and molested her pre-teen charges: Spencer believed himself in love, and only later realised he was the victim of “a voracious paedophile”.

A Very Private School makes it clear, without pussyfooting around or apparently fearing any accusations of “wokery”, that such schools were explicitly designed to “populate and replenish the ranks” of the British Empire. A homesick child would have “his stiff upper lip cast in the furnace of English boarding school life, where his emotions were cauterised,” writes Earl Spencer. “The resultant, desensitised functionary could be reliably deployed far from home – whether in Calcutta, Cape Town or Calgary.”

He also touches upon the vexed question of why more children didn’t tell their parents what was happening at school, and why so many parents continued to perpetuate the boarding school tradition. “I suspect a simple reflex,” is Earl Spencer’s main theory – it was just the done thing, he suggests. It would have been interesting to read more about this, though it is now too late, or in some cases seemingly too painful, for parents to face the consequences of doing what they thought best.

Our sympathy for royals and aristos moaning about their upbringing can be a little thin – especially when, as in this case, they throw in a load of therapy-speak (see also: Harry, and Spare). But that really shouldn’t be our reaction here: while the practices at Maidwell sound Victorian, they were happening in the 70s. This is our recent history – and, as with child abuses in institutions such as the church or children’s homes, they must be brought into the light. The fact that parents paid handsomely for their children to be brutalised should not diminish the horror of it.

Published on Thursday by HarperCollins (£25)
topics: Book Reviews, Books, Private Schools, Royal Family

title: Mortgage deals increase by hundreds of pounds a year as lenders pull cheaper rates
body:
Brokers say the speed at which rates are being pulled is a 'joke' and some customers are missing out on the best deals

Lenders are pulling mortgage rates at the quickest rate for six months, with customers facing costs totalling hundreds of pounds per year more a result.

The average shelf-life of a mortgage has nearly halved since the start of February, according to data from Moneyfacts, with the average deal on the market for only 15 days before being pulled, compared to 28 days, which it was a month ago.

Mortgages were last being taken off the market this quickly in September 2023, with the lowest average on record being 12 days – recorded last summer.

At the moment, mortgage prices are broadly increasing, with lenders tending to replace their rates with more expensive ones.

The average five-year fixed rate mortgage is currently at 5.35 per cent, which is up from 5.18 per cent at the start of February, according to Moneyfacts.

For a borrower with a £250,000 mortgage, this would mean monthly payments of £1,512 instead of £1,487 – which is £25 per month or £300 per year more.

Halifax, Santander and NatWest have all announced price increases this week, with several lenders reversing the cuts they made back in January, when expectations were that the Bank of England base rate would fall soon, and at a faster rate than economists now expect.

Experts have said the speed at which deals are pulled has become a “joke,” and that it has become difficult for homeowners to keep track of all the changes.

Brokers say that in certain cases banks are changing prices twice in a week and that customers who do not finish their paperwork on time are facing higher costs as a result.

Mark Robinson, managing director at Albion Forest Mortgages, said: “Some rates are being changed twice a week at the moment, meaning by the time an adviser has sent a quote to someone, and then gone through it with them, the lender might have pulled the rate.”

Lewis Shaw of Shaw Financial Services added: “Changes in the mortgage market happen rapidly with very little notice. The issues start when rates are constantly changing and people aren’t providing documents in a timely manner. This often leads to a higher mortgage rate at the moment and hits buyers in their pockets.”

Justin Moy, of EHF Mortgages, said that the 15-day average did not tell the full story, with many lenders changing deals even more quickly.

“It feels like products are with us for hours, not days. It may be when you are looking across the whole market, there is enough movement from all the lenders that gives us that optical illusion of 15 days,” he said.

He said brokers needed at least 24 hours’ notice before a change to allow them to deliver “proper advice.”

Imran Hussain, director at Harmony Financial Services, said the speed of change was causing “nothing but stress” for buyers as well as brokers.

“The time products are available has become a joke more recently,” he said.

In January, multiple lenders were offering sub-4 per cent deals – with HSBC taking rates to a low of 3.94 per cent for those with large amounts of equity or large deposits, though deals have worsened since then.

Fixed-rate mortgage pricing is based on Swap rates, with bigger lenders generally cutting or upping mortgage pricing around two weeks after changes to these rates.

Swap rates follow long-term predictions of where the Bank of England base rate will go next. The rate is currently at 5.25 per cent, which is a 15-year high.

Late in 2023, some traders predicted rates could fall in March – with the Bank of England’s panel of economists meeting next week – though these predictions have now been tempered, with some forecasters pushing the expected date of a rate cutback.

The Centre for Economics and Business Research (CEBR) previously told i it was forecasting a rate cut in May, but now says it will probably be June.

Many households have been struggling when they come to remortgage or buy a property after the Bank of England base rate rose from 0.1 per cent to 5.25 per cent over the past few years.

But the Budget featured very little in terms of policy that affected housing, with those under consideration – such as a scheme to back mortgages for people with a deposit of just 1 per cent – not making into the final document.
topics: Bank Of England, Fixed-rate mortgage, Mortgage, Mortgages, Property

title: ‘I schedule sex in our Google calendar – I treat it like going to the gym’
body:
If we add the rest of our lives to our shared calendar, why do we resist putting intimacy in? Lucy Denyer looks at the benefits

Chrissy Teigen is a fan. Vanessa Feltz reportedly looks forward to it once a week. And Joe Wicks has credited it to keeping the romance alive in his marriage. No, it’s not a really good massage, or the joy of taking out the bins, it’s scheduled sex. In the diary, on this date, we’ve agreed in advance that we will get it on.

“Frankly, scheduling is often the only way it’s going to happen,” admits one midlife mother-of-three friend, who’s been (happily) married to her husband for more than 20 years. And she adds, “If it’s something you can look forward to, you go and get your bottle of wine and you might actually have a shower. It’s a good thing.”

She’s not the only one at it: raising the subject with friends, it turns out that most of them have some sort of schedule going on. For one who works on Sundays but has Fridays off, Thursday night is sex night. Another friend has taken to doing it on a Friday at lunchtime: she has the day off; her husband works from home that day; their youngest is at nursery for three hours. “It means that in the evening I can just have my dinner and go to bed,” she laughs. “Doing it in the daytime takes the pressure off.”

Another friend likens pre-planned sex to going to the gym or putting the bins out: not necessarily something she feels like doing in advance, but is always glad about after. Another agrees: “I almost never feel like going for a run but I know how good it makes me feel, and it’s often the same with sex.”

This isn’t totally new: one former colleague remembers her parents doing this – she was sent to Sunday school every week with her sister not because her family was particularly religious but because that was their sex time.

I confess I’m not immune to such behaviour. A few years ago, my husband and I went through a phase of putting sex appointments in our shared Google calendar and making a point of inviting the other to attend. The deal was that we had to accept, and we had to follow through.

It might sound deeply unromantic,but in fact, according to sex therapist Cyndi Darnell, in a busy life where we schedule everything from grocery shopping to catching up with friends, “it stands to reason that if we think sex is important, we’ll schedule it”.

“Scheduling sex is one of the only ways that sexual intimacy can happen in long term relationships when you have so much stuff going on,” agrees sex therapist Gigi Engle. More importantly, she adds, doing so “is about valuing and nurturing the sexual connection you have with your partner”. She says: “It’s not because sex is so boring and bad that you have to put it on the calendar, but because you’re saying it’s so important that you are making time to do it.”

To sit around and wait for desire to hit like a lightning bolt, says Engle, misunderstands how desire manifests itself, especially in long-term relationships. “I can pretty much guarantee that with any long-term relationship, if you sit around and wait for spontaneity, you’re not going to have sex,” she says. Or as one friend wryly puts it: “If as a couple you wait for the stars to align, when everyone feels like it and you’re not too tired and there’s clean sheets on the bed and all the kids are asleep – well, there are just too many obstacles. Sometimes you have to just do it.”

Planning it in advance also means you’re more likely to be responsive, because you’re open to the idea of becoming turned on, and valuing that connection in advance. And if you still feel as if putting sex on the calendar is putting way too much advance thought into things, remember, says Engle, that sex at the beginning of a relationship is arguably the most pre-planned of all – because “you’ve been thinking about the date all day, planning what to wear, you know you’re probably going to end up in bed. So actually, that ‘spontaneous’ sex is more planned than we think”.

Ready to start syncing your calendar? There are some important things to remember. “We can’t schedule bad sex and think that’s going to be an antidote to any sort of problem,” warns Cyndi Darnell. “Thinking ‘I’ve got 30 minutes on Wednesday night let’s hope for the best’ is the opposite of connection.” We have to remove the emphasis on penetrative sex for a start, she says, and think instead about scheduling time together for connection, which might mean lying in bed to watch a movie together, and taking a joint bath, or just sitting and talking.

If you do want to get a bit fruity, “the only definition of sex should be that both people are getting pleasure and are happy to be there”, says Engle. “That can include massage, oral sex, masturbation together, cuddling naked – no one sexual act is better than any other.”

It’s worth considering some practicalities: if you work Monday-Friday, 9-5, weeknight sex scheduling may just end up with mutual disappointment because you’re both knackered; think instead about sending the kids over to Grandma’s on a Saturday afternoon or Sunday morning. And physically putting it in a shared calendar, at the same time every week, is also a good idea: doing so signals that you’re committing to set aside time for intimacy and connection.

Having it there to anticipate can also give an opportunity to build up the foreplay, by sending flirty texts and thinking about the things you’re going to do, says Engle: “It’s carving out time for your relationship.”

Had a fight or missed the sex appointment? Don’t beat yourself up. “Shit happens – and we don’t always make spin class every week either,” acknowledges Engle. But if you’ve had a fight, she says, “then use the time to connect and try and figure out how you can get back on the same page”.

I admit that, having fallen out of the calendar habit but actually taking a good look at my diary, there’s an awful lot of stuff in there, but barely any time that’s ringfenced time for me and my husband to just hang out. So often we end up giving each other the dregs of our day, or filling our weekends up with family activities or time with other people – a far cry from the early days of our relationship. I’ve vowed to reset that, and to prioritise quality time with him, regardless of where it might end up. That calendar invitation is going back in.
topics: Features, Sex, Sex And Relationships

title: I live in the Streatham LTN – it was a disaster and I’m glad it’s gone
body:
The Streatham 'low traffic neighbourhood' scheme was supposed to reduce traffic but left buses taking two hours to travel three miles. Claire Cohen asks - are LTNs compatible with cities?

Events in my small corner of Streatham in south London don’t normally warrant front page news, unless you count the recent refurb of Budgens. But in the last couple of months, we’ve become the talk of the town, and gone from unremarkable to decidedly controversial, thanks to a bitterly opposed low traffic neighbourhood (LTN) scheme that was introduced last October.

Last week we were told that Lambeth Council has decided to suspend the scheme, with immediate effect and way before the end of its 12 to 18-month deadline.

Within days of its launch, it had been clear to many local people that what was intended to reduce the volume of cars on residential streets near Streatham High Road (less flatteringly known as the A23 and one of the major routes out of London) was having a serious knock-on effect.

The most obvious was the major traffic jams. With once vital through-roads closed off to vehicles, they were being pushed onto the main arteries through Streatham. At times there were 20 buses stuck back-to-back, with nowhere to go. Transport for London data showed that one bus took 121 minutes to travel 2.9 miles – a route scheduled to last 29 minutes. It would have been twice as quick to walk. It got so bad that buses were being diverted at peak times to avoid gridlock.

My local bus to and from the high street, which usually takes less than 10 minutes at rush-hour, was suddenly more like a 30 minute journey – meaning I stopped catching it so regularly when coming home after dark. So much for all those pledges to make the capital’s streets feel safer for women and girls.

Meanwhile, the congestion meant that cars would often speed through traffic lights after they’d turned red – one narrowly missed me and I slammed its boot in anger as it sped past. I’m probably lucky the driver didn’t stop.

Tensions ran high elsewhere. On Valley Road, one of those formerly important cut-throughs newly deemed a LTN zone, vigilantes in hi-vis jackets patrolled the tarmac, warning anyone who hadn’t spotted the tiny laminated sign at the entrance that going any further would incur a £130 fine. I saw elderly locals out there, in all weathers, handing out leaflets to drivers. LTN signs were regularly vandalised and locals feel that crime has increased on the quieter roads.

And don’t mention school pick-ups. The local primary school was up in arms about the congestion, with parents unable to collect their children on time and those that travelled by public transport getting later and later. Many felt the pollution on the main roads had increased, with some children complaining of headaches while sitting in traffic jams.

You didn’t have to be local to feel the impact, either. Tradespeople found it so difficult to get to jobs that many stopped coming into the zone, missing out on work. Delivery drivers have boycotted. And trying to get an Uber home has been near-impossible. One friend was in a taxi, when the driver got out of the car and put a plastic bag over the numberplate, so he could drive through the LTN without incurring a fine.

This was a disaster that united the local community in opposition. In fact, the only winners seem to be the council – which made £320,000 in fines over the first three months of the operation. Within minutes of the announcement, my phone was beeping with messages from local friends and neighbours. “Good news!” wrote my 71-year-old pal, Liz, who had struggled to get to important medical appointments, stuck in gridlocked traffic for hours at a time.

Cycling and walking campaigners have called it a “backwards step” but the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said it was the “right thing”. He and others have said problems were exacerbated by utility companies carrying out works on roads in the area.

We all want to reduce air pollution. But are LTNs really the solution? If the idea was to encourage people onto public transport – well, that was a massive fail, as the infrastructure simply isn’t in place. And it’s not just the capital: an LTN scheme has been abandoned in Newcastle for similar reasons, while frustrated locals in Exeter, Brighton and Oxford have angrily protested against them.

Lambeth Council has doubled down on the positive impact, saying there had been “an average 60 per cent decrease in traffic”, although “an eight per cent increase in traffic on boundary roads”. But it claims to have listened to the people (eventually) and is now going to encourage Transport for London to implement cycle and walking schemes, as well as bus priority lanes. It’s almost like London has an election coming up.
topics: Features, Pollution, Traffic

title: Pet owners ‘overpaying’ to get treatment for their animals
body:
Vets face formal investigation after regulator voices concerns about pricing and competition

Pet owners could be overpaying for medicine or treatments for their animals, the competition watchdog has warned.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said thousands of worried pet owners said they struggled to find basic information including basic price lists.

The regulator has decided to launch a formal market investigation which could allow it to intervene directly in the sector.

The CMA, which launched a review last year over concerns that people could be paying too much, received more than 50,000 responses from concerned owners.

The vet industry is worth £2bn after pet ownership rose to two-thirds of UK households during the pandemic, according to the CMA.

It said it is worried that owners may not be able to get enough information to make informed decisions over care for their animals.

It found sales of medicines make up almost a quarter of the income of some practices and there was little incentive to see that clients were informed of other options such as taking their prescriptions to a cheaper provider.

The watchdog has questioned whether the regulatory framework for vets may be outdated and no longer fit for purpose.

It also questioned whether the consolidation of the market by six major veterininary firms has resulted in insufficient competition. Almost a third of Britain’s 5,000 vet practices have been bought by six firms since 2013 – CVS Group, IVC, Linnaeus, Medivet, Pets at Home and VetPartners – according to the CMA.

Sarah Cardell, CMA chief executive, said: “We launched our review of the veterinary sector last September because this is a critical market for the UK’s 16 million pet owners.

“The unprecedented response we received from the public and veterinary professionals shows the strength of feeling on this issue is high and why we were right to look into this.

“We have heard concerns from those working in the sector about the pressures they face, including acute staff shortages, and the impact this has on individual professionals.

“But our review has identified multiple concerns with the market that we think should be investigated further. Given these strong indications of potential concern, it is time to put our work on a formal footing.”

If a formal investigation upholds its findings, it would give the CMA the power to compel companies to give it a full set of information about its business and prices, impose limits on prices for things like prescription fees, and potentially even enforce the sale of certain businesses.

Dr Anna Judson, President of the British Veterinary Association, welcomed the CMA inquiry saying the veterinary sector has ‘changed significantly over recent years’.

“Rising prices are a concern for everyone but it’s vital to recognise there is no NHS for pets. Whether they are employed by corporate or independently owned practices, vets deliver highly specialised, tailored care for the UK’s pets and the cost is a fair reflection of investment in medical equipment, supplies and medicines, and the time vet teams dedicate to the care of each patient,” she said.

The BVA wanted to see “healthy competition and consumer choice” and were already supporting vet practices to be more transparent over their costs and who owns them. “It’s important that clients have as wide a choice of vet practices as possible so they can find a service that best suits the needs of themselves and their animals.

“We’re pleased to see the CMA acknowledging the need for reform of the outdated Veterinary Surgeons Act and for regulation of vet practices, something we have been calling for. As the legislation stands, it’s not fit for purpose and is failing both vet teams and clients.”

Shares in some vet groups fell after the CMA report. One of them, Pets at Home, said it is disappointed with the CMA’s findings and does not think its business model reduces competition.

A spokeswoman for the group said: “Whilst our brand is national, our veterinary practices are led by individual entrepreneurial vets who have clinical and operational freedom.

“They choose all pricing, products and services to ensure the best care for clients and their much-loved pets in their local area, which promotes competition in the market and helps to keep prices low.

“We have been working closely with the CMA on their areas of concern and will continue to do so as their inquiry progresses to ensure the distinctiveness of our model is fully recognised.”
topics: Competition, Pets, Vets

title: No, Kate did not use her Vogue cover in her family portrait – here’s how to tell
body:
Wild conspiracy theories have been shared online about the Princess of Wales as she recovers from abdominal surgery

Every now and then, a photograph grips the nation. This time there’s two.

The latest development in the ‘Katespiracy’ saga is an unfounded claim that the Princess of Wales’s 2016 Vogue shoot was reused in the now infamous Mother’s Day photo.

But analysis by i of the photo released by Kensington Palace on Sunday shows that it is extremely unlikely that Kate’s face was lifted from the magazine cover that was shot eight years ago.

It comes after international photo agencies pulled the image of Kate and her three children over concerns it had been manipulated. The Princess of Wales later apologised and indicated that “like many amateur photographers”, she had edited the image.

The events have further fuelled wild conspiracy theories that have been shared online about Kate as she recovers from the abdominal surgery she had in January. One post on X, formerly known as Twitter, about the Vogue theory has been seen more than 35 million times.

my analysis of the kate middleton photo saga is that they took her face from the vogue cover she did years ago and edited it in pic.twitter.com/JLXts08zp5— Ruby Naldrett (@rubynaldrett)

The post is from a senior social media editor for a UK national newspaper, who has faded the image of Kate from the Vogue shoot by photographer Josh Olins over the Mother’s Day photo, suggesting they are the same image.

BREAKING NEWS: The Duchess of Cambridge is Vogue’s centenary issue cover star #Vogue100 https://t.co/zkK3HWMuDO pic.twitter.com/NPbtayn7rH— British Vogue (@BritishVogue)

However, when i placed the two images next to each other and rotated the Mother’s Day image to align Kate’s head with her pose from the Vogue cover, the lighting was found to be completely different.
