The light in the Vogue image on the left hits the left hand side of her face. The light in the Mother’s Day photo on the right picks up Kate’s features on the right hand side of her face.

Part of the problem is that by fading the image in and out, as many on social media have done, smaller details which are vital in image verification are much more challenging to see.

A more effective way to attempt to verify images is to use a slider, like this one.

The most obvious difference between the two images is Catherine’s eyes. The reflection of the light is in a different place in each eye. Her eyelashes and eyebrows are different, as is her make-up.

The lines around her mouth are also different. And in the photo released on Sunday, more of the bottom row of her teeth are visible compared with the 2016 picture.

The edits to the Mother’s Day photo that Kate has indicated she was responsible for point to an obvious and far less salacious reality than many on social media would prefer.

The image released on Sunday appears that it could be a number of photos from the same shoot layered and merged in Adobe Photoshop, photo editing software used by many professionals. This is sometimes done by photographers who want to ensure every person in the photo looks their best, something not totally uncommon in photos with children, who can be harder to manage.

For example, if the photographer ends up with a series of photos when the children are not smiling in the same shot, images can be spliced together to show all the children smiling in the same photo.

The Mother’s Day image of Kate and her three children, issued over the weekend, was pulled by photo agencies amid fears it was manipulated, sparking widespread speculation about the origins of the photo and allegations it may have been faked.

One of the agencies, the Associated Press, said the “source had manipulated the image” in a way that did not meet its standards.

The Princess of Wales, who has been out of the public eye following abdominal surgery, apologised for “confusion” over the photo.

In a statement issued almost 24 hours after the portrait was released, she appeared to take personal responsibility for altering the image.

Many observers noticed several legitimate issues with the photo, including fading around Princess Charlotte’s jumper cuff and misaligned tiles on the floor.
topics: Princess of Wales, Royal Family, Vogue

title: ‘I was a royal photographer – Princess of Wales’s picture shows why they need professionals’
body:
Ian Lloyd, a biographer and ex-royal photographer, says the Princess is the only frontline royal he knows who has edited their own images

A former royal photographer believes controversy over the Princess of Wales’s official Mother’s Day picture has shown younger members of the Royal Family why they must still outsource the editing of their images to professionals.

Ian Lloyd said Kate, a keen amateur photographer who studied history of art at St Andrews University, is the only front-rank royal he knows who has edited their own images.

Mr Lloyd, who has photographed royals including the late Queen and the Duke of Edinburgh, said historically members of the Royal Family had instructed official photographers such as Sir Cecil Beaton to ensure favourable images were used but had not taken part in the post-production process.

Kate was forced to apologise after international photo agencies pulled the image after it emerged it had been manipulated. It was the first authorised image of the Princess of Wales since she underwent abdominal surgery in January.

Mr Lloyd said the furore over the editing of a family shot of Kate, Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis showed that the palace should ensure any editing should not be done by royals again.

“I think they should probably outsource it to somebody that is a top professional and who is capable, but also discreet,” Mr Lloyd told i.

“Or get somebody to come in and share the images and look at them and discuss them.

“You’ve got to find a secure company or an individual that’s used to dealing with state politicians or top notch-celebrities.

“I think their aim was to create an intimacy with the viewer – ‘this is what we’ve created, and you’ll be doing yours at home today but this is what we’ve done’.”

While Kate would probably continue to explore her interest in photography privately, anything for public consumption from now on will have to be “squeaky clean”, he added.

“Or else everybody will ignore the photograph, zooming in to see what has been done to it,” he said.

On Monday, the Princess of Wales apologised for “confusion” over the photograph shared by Kensington Palace which was pulled by photo agencies after claims it was manipulated.

Royal sources said the Princess of Wales made “minor adjustments” and that Kate and Prince of Wales wanted to offer an informal picture of the family together for Mother’s Day.

Insiders have told The Times that Kate felt “awful” about it she had just “tried to make it the best it could be” because she knew how important it was for it to be “a nice picture”. Mr Lloyd, who photographed nearly all the Queen Mother’s engagements for more than 20 years, said the princess’s editing of the image was “unwise”.

But she may have been able to capture a family image that professionals can’t, with sitting for photographers sometimes “intimidating” for royals.

“She can capture the moment because the moment is the most important thing, “he said.

“I’ve read lots of people’s accounts of photographing the royals. It’s very difficult because you photograph somebody who’s not co-operative and not able to relax.

“Children are very difficult to to get to respond in that way and the fact she managed to get her three children roaring with laughter and looking at the camera was an achievement.”

The decision by five photo agencies to issue a “kill” notice on the photo because of concerns the image had been doctored has led to questions about the media’s handling of royal photographs.

But the “insatiable interest” for royal pics meant the press and the royals “need each other”.

“The media … need these good royal stories to boost circulation. And the royalty needs the media to get that message out there,” he said.

“If I were them, I’d probably talk to editors, and the agencies themselves, get the palace to talk to them and decide really what would work. Which is what Diana did really during the war of the Wales’s in the 90s.”

Dr Ed Owens, a royal historian and commentator, said the Royal Family had been producing a form of “soft propaganda” for years.

“At no point has the media stood up and said, ‘We’re not going to simply accept the narrative’,” he said.

“They know that the Royal Family has, historically at least, been popular with the British public. Ensuring that they can report on the Royal Family in a way that gives the public access to the lives of these individuals has been the priority of the press historically.

“What I would hope will be the outcome is that we do start to hear from a wider section of the media a greater scepticism, about official images, official narratives produced by the Royal Family for public consumption.”
topics: Prince George, Princess of Wales, Royal Family, William, Prince of Wales

title: Boeing black box data to be seized after Dreamliner ‘freezes’ mid-flight leaving 50 hurt
body:
New Zealand’s aviation authority says it will seize cockpit data. Passengers were left injured after the jet went into 'free fall'

New Zealand’s aviation authority has said it would seize the cockpit voice and flight data recorders from the Sydney to Auckland flight on which 50 people were injured after it “froze” in mid-air, as passengers criticised Latam Airlines for a lack of communication following the incident.

The Boeing 787 carrying 263 passengers and nine crew from Sydney to Auckland abruptly dropped during the flight on Monday, sending passengers flying and leaving several bleeding and with broken bones.

Fifty people had to be treated by ambulance crews upon arrival in Auckland with 13 requiring hospital treatment. Four people had to stay in hospital for a second night on Tuesday, according to the New Zealand Herald.

Passengers recounted seeing people with blood streaming from their heads, while some reported broken arms, shoulders and ribs. The injured passengers were from Brazil, France, Australia, Chile and New Zealand.

Brian Adam Jokat, a Canadian citizen who lives in the UK, told Reuters he was shocked to see a person in the seat next to him thrown up in the air.

“My neighbour who was in the seat two over from me, there was a gap in between us, as soon as I woke I looked and he was on the ceiling and I thought I was dreaming,” he said.

Another woman told the Herald: “I used to be a flight attendant and this is the first time I’ve ever … the whole plane just froze.”

New Zealand’s Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC) said on Tuesday the accident occurred in international airspace and Chile’s Dirección General de Aeronáutica Civil (DGAC) had opened an investigation. The TAIC is working to assist the inquiry, including gathering the so-called “black boxes” that reveal the flight’s trajectory and communication between pilots.

Latam, which is based in Chile, said it would assist authorities investigating what caused the “strong movement” on the flight. It sent an email to passengers expressing “sincere apologies for the situation” and offering to reimburse them for any expenses.

“We are committed, and it is our top priority to assist all our passengers. We want to assure you that we are here to support you,” it said, according to the New Zealand Herald.

“If you have not received access to accommodations, food, ground transportation, or if you incurred any other expense as a result of this situation, we ask that you please provide us with the documentation associated with these expenses for the reimbursement review process,” the email said.

However, it is understood the company did not offer a refund for the flight and passengers said they were given a single McDonald’s cheeseburger after the ordeal.

Clara Azevedo, a 28-year-old from Brisbane in Australia, said the plane went into “free fall” until the pilot managed to regain control. She said the airline had not offered her any help and she spent the night in hospital translating for a 68-year-old woman who broke two ribs.

“We are all traumatised, and we had to find strength to help people out. But this is not our responsibility, it is Latam’s – but they haven’t done anything. That’s very frustrating,” she told the New Zealand Herald.

Latam has been contacted for comment.

More than 300 passengers due to fly with the airline from Auckland to Santiago, Chile on Tuesday spoke of their anxiety about travelling after the unexplained incident.

“I popped my head out to look back and it looked like people had been through war,” said Colombian citizen Larry Reef about the flight on Monday. He was due to board Tuesday night’s flight and said he was worried but “had to get back on the horse”.

“Fingers crossed lightning doesn’t strike twice,” he said.

The incident comes as Boeing faces questions over its 737 series in recent years. In January, it came under intense scrutiny after an unused cabin door on one of its 737s was blown off at 16,000 ft. On Monday, the company hit headlines after a former employee turned whistleblower was found dead in the US.

Guy Gratton, associate professor of aviation and the environment at Cranfield University, told i that Monday’s accident was still a “surprise”.

“There is a particular history with the Boeing 737 Max family of aircraft, that’s a completely different aircraft design albeit from the same company,” he said.

“The Boeing 787 has a great safety track record, so there’s nothing that makes you look at this and say, ‘Oh, no, not another one. This is a very surprising accident,” he said, adding that the incident could have been down to the weather, technical failure of the aircraft or mishandling by the crew.
topics: Airlines, Boeing, Flights, New Zealand

title: Inside the life of John Barnett, who blew the whistle on Boeing over safety risks
body:
The former Boeing employee claimed the company's manufacturing processes for its 787 Dreamliner aircraft were not up to standard

A former Boeing employee who claimed the company’s manufacturing processes for its 787 Dreamliner aircraft were not up to standard has been found dead in his truck, according to authorities.

John Barnett, 62, died from a “self-inflicted” wound on Saturday, the Charleston County coroner in South Carolina confirmed.

His lawyer, Brian Knowles, expressed doubts over the circumstances of his death while referring to “alleged” self-inflicted wounds.

Mr Knowles said in an email to Corporate Crime Reporter that his client had been in the middle of a whistleblower lawsuit against Boeing when he was “tragically” found dead.

Mr Barnett had worked for the plane manufacturer for 32 years, until 2017, and made a series of allegations about the firm in 2019.

He died on day three of his deposition in a whistleblower lawsuit against Boeing, his lawyer said, as the former Boeing worker alleged retaliation by the US multinational over claims he made about the way it operates.

Boeing has rejected the accusations, the BBC reports.

When he failed to show up for related questioning in Charleston, South Carolina, on Saturday, inquiries were made with the hotel he was staying at. He was then reportedly found in his truck in the hotel’s car park.

Mr Barnett had worked at Boeing’s North Charleston plant since 2010, when he took on a job as quality manager in the manufacturing of 787 Dreamliners.

News of his death came on the same day that at least 50 passengers were injured when a 787-9 aircraft heading from Sydney, Australia, to Auckland, New Zealand, “froze” in mid-air after suffering a fault.

Boeing has faced scrutiny over its safety record since two fatal crashes involving the Boeing 737 Max in 2018 and 2019.

In January this year, it came under renewed pressure after an unused cabin door on one of its 737s was blown off at 16,000 ft.

Asked whether 737s could be trusted following the terrifying incident, Mr Barnett told TMZ: “One, this is not a 737 problem, it’s a Boeing problem”.

He said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was doing “due diligence and inspections to ensure the door closes on the 737 are installed properly and the fasteners are stored properly”. But he said he was worried about the condition the rest of the plane was in.

Mr Barnett said he was concerned about “jobs not being completed properly, inspection steps being removed”. He told TMZ he feared the 737 and 787 programmes “have really put a strong effort into removing quality from the process”.

In 2019, the whistleblower told the BBC that workers under pressure had deliberately fitted planes with sub-standard parts and that passengers on its 787 Dreamliner could be left without oxygen in the event of a sudden decompression.

Mr Barnett said he was concerned a push to get new aircraft built meant safety was compromised, the BBC reported.

The company denied his claims.

In a statement, Boeing said: “We are saddened by Mr Barnett’s passing, and our thoughts are with his family and friends.”

The office of Charleston County Coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said: “Charleston City Police Department is the investigating agency. No further details are available at this time.”
topics: Aviation, Boeing

title: Enough is enough! Leave the Royals and their children alone
body:
Let’s imagine for a moment that you are trying to recover from major surgery in the privacy of your home, while keeping an eye on your three young children, all of whom are still very much dependent on you.

You are scrolling through your phone and you find that the world is speculating over whether you have done a Gone Girl and disappeared or left your husband (even though your office has issued an official statement to say, in no uncertain terms, that you will be out of action until Easter, which is still, let’s not forget, almost three weeks away).

As a fellow mum of three, with children of a similar age, I know how hard it is to take so much as a day off. I can only imagine how difficult it is for the Princess of Wales to rest and recover when she has, involuntarily, found herself in the eye of a media storm.

Is it really any wonder, then, that our future queen, who spends the majority of her life shaking hands and smiling at the public, in between campaigning for better support for children in their early years and residing over 20 charitable and military organisations, posted a picture on Mother’s Day to try and quell some of the frenzied speculation? I should think she’s thoroughly sick of it by now.

And so what if Kate, who describes herself as an amateur photographer, got a bit carried away and overedited the picture of Prince George, 10, Princess Charlotte, eight, and Prince Louis, five, in the process? Let’s not forget she is supposed to be resting, not posing for pictures.

Isn’t it a bit much for the world to be focusing so carefully on a picture of three young kids anyway? I’m not averse to sharing pictures of my kids online but I certainly wouldn’t want people poring over these pictures as closely as we have of that Mother’s Day image the royals shared.

We seem to have overlooked, in all this furore, the simple fact that they are humans. Kate is recovering from an operation – which must have been quite serious for a hospital stay of almost two weeks – and her children, who no doubt missed their mum while she was in hospital, are trying to manage without her. Things must already be quite unsettling and turbulent for them.

And now, in light of Sunday’s photo, which has been broadcast across the world, the children are also in the spotlight with their mother. I really feel for them. They have, so far, managed to keep out of all the drama and conspiracy theories surrounding Kate’s whereabouts, despite the fact that Prince William made a gallant effort to do the school run for the first few weeks when Kate was recovering. Can you imagine the speculation at the school gates? The rumour mill must be going wild.

I bet all the children at their school have been instructed by their parents not to ask but you know how terrible children are at keeping secrets. I bet the questions are flying back and forth on Roblox. It must be very hard for Prince George and Princess Charlotte to keep quiet about what has been going on. Children are, in my experience, incredibly intuitive and they must know that everyone has been talking about their family.

As if the shame of having Great Uncle Gary going into the Big Brother house (now, mercifully, evicted) wasn’t bad enough.

The most recent statement, released by the Princess of Wales earlier yesterday (11 March) reads: “Like many amateur photographers, I do occasionally experiment with editing. I wanted to express my apologies for any confusion the family photograph we shared yesterday caused. I hope everyone celebrating had a very happy Mother’s Day”.

So just a minor oversight then. But one that has caused global news agencies to “kill” the photograph.

Does anyone else think that perhaps it would be best if we just left her and her children, who haven’t asked for any of this, alone for a while? Let’s not add to Kate or her children’s stress in the meantime by all this frenzied speculation. Enough is enough.
topics: Princess of Wales, Royal Family

title: How Premier League’s new FFP rules may affect Chelsea, Newcastle and Aston Villa
body:
Proposed changes to profit and sustainability rules (PSR) could have a huge impact on some of the top flight's biggest teams

Financial fair play, or FFP, has been a key theme of the Premier League this season.

Everton, Nottingham Forest and Manchester City are all currently under investigation for breaching the top flight’s FFP equivalent, profit and sustainability rules (PSR), while the Toffees have already been deducted six points, down from 10 after an appeal.

But it appears these rules, which have been criticised for being unclear and outdated, are now changing.

Here’s everything you need to know about the proposed PSR changes and how it’ll affect some of the clubs currently closest to breaching the original rules.

Let’s start with a recap of the current PSR rules. Among a slew of anti-corruption regulations is the key one teams are at the greatest risk of breaching – that clubs can only lose a maximum of £105m across any three-year period.

Now, it’s not quite that simple – you can deduct “healthy” expenditure like academy and women’s team investment from your losses, so teams can technically lose more than £105m.

But this is the rule Everton have breached and Forest are charged with breaching, while Manchester City’s 115 charges relate more to the anti-corruption regulations.

The latter are unlikely to substantially change, but the £105m limit is set to be scrapped altogether and replaced by a squad cost ratio, in line with Uefa’s financial sustainability rules (FSR), the successor to FFP.

A squad cost ratio is simply calculated – you divide any club’s first-team wage budget, transfer amortisation costs and agents’ fees by its overall revenue

FSR is currently winding down year-on-year to a squad-cost ratio of 70 per cent as the limit, starting with 90 per cent in 2023-24, before decreasing to 80 per cent in 2024-25.

The Premier League are reportedly aiming for a relatively generous 85 per cent squad cost ratio, meaning clubs just need to have their wage budget and amortisation costs below 85 per cent of their revenue.

It’s important to note that while clubs have agreed on a change to the regulations, it is currently unclear whether they will be introduced at the league’s AGM in June.

And any of these changes would not impact the current charges against City, Everton or Nottingham Forest, who will still be tried under the current regulations.

A Premier League statement released on Monday read: “At a Premier League shareholders’ meeting, clubs agreed to prioritise the swift development and implementation of a new league-wide financial system.

“This will provide certainty for clubs in relation to their future financial plans and will ensure the Premier League is able to retain its existing world-leading investment to all levels of the game.

“Alongside this, Premier League clubs also reconfirmed their commitment to securing a sustainably-funded financial agreement with the EFL, subject to the new financial system being formally approved by clubs.

“The league and clubs also reaffirmed their ongoing and longstanding commitment to the wider game which includes £1.6 billion distributed to all levels of football across the current three-year cycle.

“The Premier League’s significant funding contributions cover all EFL clubs and National League clubs, as well as women and girls’ football, and the grassroots of the game.”

There are probably fans of every Premier League club who want to know how changes to PSR will affect their teams, but none so more than Chelsea.

And for once this season, it’s good news for the Blues – Mauricio Pochettino’s side would probably be the biggest winners from this rule change.

As football finance expert Rob Wilson told i last week, Chelsea need to sell over £100m before the end of June to comply with PSR in its current state.

Yet because Chelsea’s revenue was announced at an all-time high of £512.5m in their 2023 accounts, a squad cost ratio would give them a lot more headroom, especially when capped at 85 per cent.

The club have been actively working to reduce their wage budget by buying younger players, who tend to demand lower salaries, which counts as a positive, compared to the £1.12bn they have spent on transfers since BlueCo bought Chelsea in May 2022.

Chelsea would comfortably fall within an 85 per cent squad cost ratio as it stands and would avoid what currently feels like an almost inevitable PSR points deduction.

This isn’t so positive in the short term but could be hugely beneficial for Newcastle United in the long term.

The Magpies’ revenue increased to £250.3m in 2022-23, a significant rise from £180m the season before, but still less than half the size of Chelsea or other “big six” sides’ turnovers.

This means they can still only spend £212.7m on wages, amortisation and agents’ fees, a figure they would currently breach by around £40m, despite their wage budget only being £187m.

These figures should also be concerning if they qualify for European competition next season, where the squad cost ratio figure decreases to 80 per cent next season.

It is believed Newcastle would currently comply with PSR in its old state, but may well be in breach if rules change.

Yet in the long term, if the Saudi-backed club continue to grow their revenue at the rate they have been and follow the model City have, the new PSR should give them much more headway to expand their playing budget and corps.

Much like Newcastle, Aston Villa are an upwardly mobile club at risk of breaching the new regulations.

Villa’s revenue this year increased to £217.7m from £178.4m, similarly to Newcastle, yet their wage costs are higher than the Magpies’ at £194.2m.

As Villa’s amortisation fees are lower than Newcastle’s over the past few years, they would likely breach a squad cost ratio by lower than their northern rivals, but crucially would still breach it by around £35m.

According to modelling by football finance expert Kieran Maguire, Newcastle and Villa are not the only teams at risk of breaching the proposed new PSR rules.

Fulham, Forest, West Ham and Wolverhampton Wanderers would all also be at risk due to their comparatively low revenues and ambitiously expensive squads.

Leeds United would also be at risk if they were to be promoted, especially given they will need to spend once they reach the Premier League.
topics: Aston Villa FC, Chelsea FC, Newcastle United FC, Premier League, Sports Explainer

title: Nash Ensemble: Terezín-Theresienstadt review: Music so poignant it’s unbearable
body:
These Czech composers murdered in the Holocaust left a gaping void in musical history. They must never be forgotten

When the Nazis turned the Czech fortress of Terezín into a concentration camp for Jews, they hadn’t planned it to be a cultural haven, but that’s what it turned into. The inhabitants seized on the freedom their gaolers gave them to create and stage their own events – even if this meant, in the words of a young Czech actress who survived, singing and dancing under the gallows. Hundreds of selected victims were taken by train every day to be gassed in Auschwitz.

The Nazis made a propaganda film about Terezín in which they depicted its sick and starving residents as enjoying a life of civilised luxury. And the centrepiece of this exercise was a rousing children’s opera entitled Brundibar.

Thanks to Simon Broughton’s classic documentary, The Music of Terezín, we can still see images from that Nazi film. In it a fictional tyrant was played by a 14-year-old boy who was evidently a promising actor. But being very small for his age, he was one of the first to be chosen for gassing, when his age-group was taken a week later to Auschwitz.

Last weekend, Broughton’s film was the springboard for a series of Terezín-related events at the Wigmore Hall, and the day was punctuated by moments of almost unbearable poignancy.

Much of the music written in Terezín perished with its composers, but enough has been preserved for us to realise that this defiant explosion of communal creativity was one of history’s most miraculous moments.

And to label Hans Krása, Pavel Haas, Gideon Klein, and the august Viktor Ullmann as “Terezín composers” is to belittle them: these were the pre-eminent voices of Czech music in the 20s and 30s, and their abrupt disappearance left a gaping void in musical history.

The presiding musical genius was the composer, conductor, and critic Viktor Ullmann, whose reviews of the nightly prison-camp concerts were as eruditely astringent as any in civilian life. To hear his music played and sung by the Nash Ensemble was to realise the greatness that was lost.

One quartet we heard had been premiered in a Terezín attic, but most powerful of all were the defiantly upbeat songs of Ilse Weber, who volunteered to die in the gas chamber, alongside her son and the sick children she had been caring for.

Broughton’s film had been commissioned by the BBC and was accompanied on its release in 1993 by a major series of Terezín concerts. Thank goodness we have the Nash Ensemble to do the same now, because the new-look BBC and the new-look Arts Council would write off this music as a hopelessly elitist effusion by dead, middle-class white men.

Simon Broughton’s film ‘The Music of Terezín’ is streaming on holocaustmusic.org
topics: Classical Music, Live Reviews

title: Wayne McGregor: ‘People think of me as an outsider, but I’ve never felt like one’
body:
Wayne McGregor is holding a glass of water aloft in his hands. He’s illustrating to me the idea of physical intelligence – how all of us, not only dancers, think with our bodies, even if we’re not wholly aware of it in our everyday lives. “When I pick up this glass,” the choreographer schools me on a video call from his home in Devon, jiggling his water tumbler from side to side, “I already know before I pick it up how heavy it’s going to be, what the calibration of the glass is, how I’m going to keep it straight to drink the water.” He tilts the glassware closer to his screen, looking intently at it. “All we’re doing in dancing is exploring that further.

“What happens when somebody picks me up?” he asks rhetorically. “I’m fascinated by that. And as the ways of understanding the body increases, the possibilities just seem more endless.”

I’ve never spoken to McGregor before, but I get the sense that this is how most of his conversations go after a few minutes of pleasantries. One minute he’s apologising about his two unhappy whippets – stuck indoors thanks to the rain. And the next, he’s rhapsodising about quantum dots and the production of light.

If you’re even vaguely familiar with McGregor’s cerebral choreography, this kind of mercurial thinking will come as no surprise. Over the past 30 years, the Stockport-born maverick – an artistic director of Studio Wayne McGregor, a resident choreographer at the Royal Ballet, and an associate artist at Sadler’s Wells – has embraced as many disciplines as he can in his desire both to question things, and to understand them.

Whether it’s directing a music video for Radiohead’s Thom Yorke, creating a ballet triptyque inspired by the writings of Virginia Woolf (titled Woolf Works), or engaging in interdisciplinary research with cognitive scientists at the Wellcome Collection (which culminated in a 2013 exhibition entitled Thinking with the Body exploring mind and movement), if there’s one word that crops up time and time again when reading about his oeuvre, it’s possibility.

Most recently, in 2022, McGregor choreographed virtual avatars in Abba Voyage, helping to create the groundbreaking digital concert by the Swedish pop group as they appeared in 1979. After five weeks of intensive filming with the septuagenarian band, McGregor used motion capture to transpose their choreographed movements onto their younger avatar selves.

It helps explain why audiences are so struck by the show’s authenticity. “Abba had a really special performance character,” McGregor said at the time. “Each member moved in a very individual way. We took that and amped it up. It makes you realise how unique we all are and how our self-expression is something to cherish.”

On a base level, he tells me, dancing has always been a way for him to understand himself. And what better way for a choreographer to understand himself than create a dance portrait sequenced by his own DNA? In 2017, McGregor began exploring the concept of the “body as archive” with Autobiography (1.0), a form of corporeal memoir that immerses itself in the idea that each cell contains multiple stories – the blueprint of a life. Choreography was created from old writings and memories. From here, 23 sections of movement were created to reflect the 23 pairs of chromosomes of the human genome, which were then fed into an algorithm based on McGregor’s genome coding.

This experimental work is set to return to Sadler’s Wells this week with a new AI tool developed with Google Arts and Culture, retitled Autobiography (v95 and v96). For every performance the algorithm selects the section of his code – and therefore the sequence of dance – that will be seen on stage. “I like that we don’t know how that piece is going to be organised,” he tells me.

Although he readily admits that this can be stressful for his dancers. When he first mentioned the concept to them, they didn’t think he’d follow through on it. “And then they realised, when we got closer and closer to it, that we weren’t abandoning,” he laughs. “It was a massive mind shift for them. How can they find joy and richness and intelligence in a system that’s so mobile?” Now they’re on their 90th performance and they’ve never danced the same thing twice.

“It’s extraordinary to watch the potential of the human body,” McGregor muses – something he calls an ecosystem: the connection between mind and matter and “its ability to change and morph”.

There is a clarity to McGregor’s approach that still feels new 18 years after he was appointed the Royal Ballet’s resident choreographer in 2006. At the time, it was considered a radical move. Unlike his predecessors, he had very little classical training. Ruffling feathers might not have been at the top of the Royal Ballet’s agenda but ruffle feathers McGregor did. A hip sticking out, an elbow dropped to the side. As Deborah Bull, a former principal dancer with the Royal Ballet, described it: “there is beauty in movements that we’d brought up to believe were ugly.”

McGregor’s birdlike undulations have come to define his wild and rule-breaking choreography: a little like morse code, the dit and the dah of his flicks and rolls. It’s a left-field approach that many have traced back to his childhood in Stockport in the 70s. At the age of seven, McGregor was lassoed into dance by the feverish hip gyrations of John Travolta on the light-up dance floor. But it was at his first ballroom classes where he was encouraged to make up his own moves. “Even though it was through ballroom, Latin American and disco dancing, I was always connected to my body,” he says of that time.

Does he tire of our constant reflection on his unorthodox entry to classical dance? “There are still some people who think I’m an outsider, which is bizarre to me,” he replies. “At the end of the day, I am working with bodies, and those bodies all share the same biomechanical principles – whether or not they’re expressed in a technique which happens to be ballet, contemporary dance or hip hop.” Which is why “I’ve never felt like an outsider, I’ve never worried about going to the Paris Opera [where he regularly creates work], because all I’m doing is working in a room of bodies that I know a lot about.”

McGregor once said that “the world isn’t complete, it’s complicated”, and this aphorism can be seen in much of his staged work: from the powerful and reflective Infra (his response to the 7/7 London bombings), to the slow-motion explosives of Live Fire Exercise (a meditation on war and trauma), and onwards to his second Sadlers Wells instalment this week, entitled UniVerse: “a modern eco-myth that asks how we can come together to be whole again.”

It is another of his works that engages with current issues, even if he doesn’t always do so explicitly. “One of the things I’m trying to do is be part-activist even if that’s under the radar and people don’t recognise it,” McGregor says. He’s tired of the conversational narrative around dance, “that it isn’t an intellectual art form and that it’s non-verbal to the extent that it just happens in the moment.” How can we communicate what dance actually is, he asks? “It’s really about staying inquisitive,” he says. “And if you’re not doing that, I think you have to question why you’re doing it and what’s the purpose.”

When it comes to the technology of the body, what is the purpose at this stage in his career, I ask – what is left to explore? The answer, as ever, is on the tip of his tongue. Augmented reality. “I’m wondering if in the future it’s going to be about screens and things that you wear,” he begins to explain, before going off on multiple tangents. What would that look like on the body? He may not have the answers just yet, but he’s in the midst of trying to find out.

Soon we’re discussing retinal tracking. Not long after that we’re into biometric signals. And just like that, we’re back down the rabbit hole. This is Wayne’s world, after all. The best I can do here is nod along – and try and keep up.

‘Autobiography (v95 and v96)’ is at Sadler’s Wells on 12 and 13 March, and ‘UniVerse: A Dark Crystal Odyssey’ on 15 and 16 March
topics: Ballet, Dance

title: Oscars 2024: The 11 biggest moments
body:
So that’s it for another year: no slaps, no surprises, Oppenheimer won everything we expected, Killers of the Flower Moon won nothing it deserved, and Bradley Cooper won, well, nothing. Sure, Hollywood’s biggest night was not the most exciting – even the dresses were unadventurous (what’s with the monochrome?) – but there was a very well-behaved dog in the audience, and the ceremony did feel like a proper, full-hearted celebration of some of the best years in film in recent memory.

There might never have been a Best Picture shortlist like it, even if Christopher Nolan ensured most of the others didn’t get a look-in. If you didn’t stay up all night to watch the “action”, we’ve got you covered.

If it seemed early in the night as though Poor Things might pull off an upset and knock bookies’ favourite Oppenheimer off its perch, that didn’t last long. Nolan’s sweeping biopic of the scientist behind the atomic bomb swept most of the big awards, its momentum building so much that by the time Al Pacino utterly fumbled his announcement of Best Picture (by mumbling it out too quickly, destroying any chance of a bit of suspense), it was something of an anti-climax. We all knew it would be Oppenheimer. And Oppenheimer it was.

There are some Hollywood bigwigs who are so big and wiggy that you assume they already have at least a couple of Oscars knocking about. Nolan is one; Robert Downey Jr is another. Shockingly, though, neither of them had a single one until last night. RDJ seemed characteristically nonchalant about his win for Oppenheimer, but I suspect it meant more than he let on, and Nolan finally won after being nominated eight times before.

Poor Things might not have toppled Oppenheimer, but there was one big shock: Lily Gladstone not winning the Oscar for Best Actress for her role as Mollie Burkhart in Martin Scorsese’s Killers of the Flower Moon (which by the way won zero of the 10 awards it was nominated for). After sweeping awards season this year, everyone expected Gladstone to make history as the first Native American woman to win an acting Oscar.

But it was Emma Stone who won, for playing the endearing infant-brain-in-adult-body Bella Baxter in Yorgos Lanthimos’s weird and wild coming-of-age story. Gladstone’s performance was devastating and restrained but I’m not at all surprised Stone won it (for the second time) – this was one of the strangest characters on film in years and after watching it, all I could think of was that Stone had acted her arse off and had a complete riot. When her name was called she looked deeply uncomfortable, which I thought was because she felt awkward for robbing Gladstone (anticipating backlash online), but might just be because she busted the zip on her dress dancing to Ryan Gosling’s Ken song.

For the fourth time, Jimmy Kimmel proved himself a safe pair of hands, which is all anyone can really hope for since Chris Rock, isn’t it? It wasn’t laugh a minute and he’s not a film buff, but Kimmel seemed relaxed and in command, save for one imprudent addiction gag about Robert Downey Jr early on that had me fearing he might not recover. He more or less did, and got a couple of half-decent shots in, though his relief that Al Pacino had found a babysitter – Pacino had a baby last summer, at the age of 83 – seemed to go over the crowd’s heads.

The most supportive reaction of the night came when he read out a less than positive social media post reviewing his performance so far. “Has there EVER been a WORSE HOST than Jimmy Kimmel at The Oscars? His opening was that of a less than average person trying too hard to be something which he is not, and never can be. Get rid of Kimmel and perhaps replace him with another washed up, but cheap, ABC ‘talent,’ George Slopanopoulos. He would make everybody on stage look bigger, stronger, and more glamorous.”

“Well, thank you, President Trump,” Kimmel replied. “Thank you for watching, I’m surprised you’re still up – isn’t it past your jail time?” Cue standing ovation and cheers.

Brits kept popping up in places both expected and not. The Zone of Interest became the first British film to win Best International Feature (it qualified because its dialogue is largely Polish and German); there were repeated wins of course for Christopher Nolan, whose work I have always thought gives off “dark brooding American” but who is in fact a mild-mannered Englishman; Sean Lennon even won an Oscar for his short film War Is Over!, inspired by his parents’ beloved Christmas song.

I lost count of the amount of British people wishing their mums a Happy Mother’s Day (including Lennon to Yoko) and probably confusing the predominantly American audience (Mother’s Day is in May in the US) in the process.

The hellish, vital documentary 20 Days in Mariupol, filmed inside the city during the early days of Russia’s invasion, became the first Ukrainian film to ever win an Oscar – and its director Mstyslav Chernov gave one of the most powerful speeches of the evening. “I wish I’d never made this film,” he said. “I wish to be able to exchange this to Russia never attacking Ukraine.”

Chernov, who also has a Pulitzer for his journalism work, went on to appeal directly to the set of stars in front of him. “I cannot change history. I cannot change the past. But we all together, you – some of the most talented people in the world – can make sure the history record is set straight and the truth will prevail and the people of Mariupol and those who have lost their lives will never be forgotten.”

Glazer has given few words this season, preferring his colleagues to do the talking while accepting awards for The Zone of Interest, which observes the domestic life of an Auschwitz commandant and his family living on the edge of the concentration camp. But he stood alone on stage as he accepted the award for Best International Feature and read an enormously moving speech about the conflict in Gaza.

“All our choices were made to reflect and confront us in the present, not to say look what they did then, rather what we do now. Our film shows where dehumanisation leads at its worst. It’s shaped all of our past and present… Right now, we stand here as men who refute their Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people. Whether the victims of October 7th in Israel, or the ongoing attack on Gaza, all the victims of this dehumanisation, how do we resist?”

It would have been nice for us to have a moment to digest Glazer’s words, but instead we went straight into Emily Blunt and Ryan Gosling doing some dated Barbenheimer badinage before saluting stunt artists. This is the Oscars – and a mercifully early and concise Oscars, too – so there’s not exactly time for contemplation. But it still felt a little in poor taste.

We also had the director of 20 Days in Mariupol played out with an instrumental version of Barbie’s “I’m Just Ken”. And after Christopher Nolan won his first Oscar for a film about the father of the atomic bomb, and gave a moving speech about how humbled he was to be part of cinema history, we got a jolly chaser of the Pirates of the Caribbean score. Is everyone okay?

Aside from Chernov and Glazer, it was a decidedly apolitical evening compared to some years, which was a surprise given the increasingly desperate situation in Gaza – the ceremony was delayed because of a pro-Palestinian protest happening outside. Some artists did choose quiet protest, though; Billie Eilish, Mark Ruffalo, Ava DuVernay, Ramy Youssef and a few others wore small, red “Artists4Ceasefire” pins.

“We’re calling for an immediate, permanent ceasefire in Gaza,” Youssef, star of Poor Things, told a red-carpet interviewer. “We’re calling for peace and justice – lasting justice – for the people of Palestine.”

Anyone who didn’t think Ryan Gosling was the real star of Barbie must surely have been disabused of this notion while watching his “I’m Just Ken” extravaganza, featuring Slash and Mark Ronson on guitars and 65 dancing Kens, and performed after Gosling had lost the award for Original Song to Billie Eilish for “What Was I Made For?”, from the same film.

Hi performance was camp, it was silly, it was fun – much like his role in the film, and what made him squarely the best thing about it.

Barbie was referenced so much throughout the night yet again that it threatened to make people forget that it barely won anything. Eilish, now onto her second Oscar (yes, she has more than Christopher Nolan), also sang, but the most powerful performance of the night was Scott George and the Osage Tribal Singers with “Wahzhazhe (A Song for My People)” from Killers of the Flower Moon.

This year, instead of clips of each nominated actor’s performance, a previous winner gave a speech paying tribute to their talent, before the winner was announced. Because the Oscars don’t already have enough speeches.

This sounds glamorous and looks good – that’s 20 former winners in total, with five all-time greats on stage at once – and the nominees certainly looked touched. But it got very tedious very quickly, and after a while it was hard for it not to start feeling insincere. Had they really all chosen these specific favourites themselves, or were they just reading off an autocue like everyone else?

Ben Kingsley really did look like he meant it when he vouched for Cillian Murphy – but then he, like all of them, did obviously win an Oscar for Best Actor himself…
topics: Academy Awards, Film, Oscars

title: Finally: an Oscars that didn’t make me angry
body:
In my lifetime of watching the Academy Awards, and my entire career as a film critic covering them, it is vanishingly rare to have basically no moment during the ceremony broadcast that either served as a big snack-break filler or made me so angry I wanted to put a boot through the television. A litany of idiotic jokes, ill-conceived musical numbers, and predictable choices have haunted the Oscars for most of my time watching them. So imagine my surprise when this year’s telecast of the Oscars was actually enjoyable.

It seems someone producing the Oscars finally realised that you should give the people what they want. And what they want is Ryan Gosling in a rhinestone-bedecked fucshia outfit and sunglasses, performing “I’m Just Ken” from his mega-hit Barbie, passing the mic to Greta Gerwig and Margot Robbie to karaoke along. What they want is Al Pacino and a cute dog (Messi, from Anatomy of a Fall) in the audience. What they want is a Twins reunion featuring Arnold Schwarzenegger and Danny DeVito.

I’d hesitate to say that what they want is to see John Cena naked, but yes, there was also that: a genuinely funny gag about the infamous Oscars streaker, featuring the wrestler/actor using an Academy envelope to maintain his dignity.

And even beyond the buoyant, non-stodgy, and amusing presentation of the show, there was the quality of the films. Unsurprisingly (but not undeservingly), Oppenheimer, Christopher Nolan’s biopic of the atomic bomb creator, swept the majority of categories, taking seven plaudits including Best Supporting Actor for Robert Downey Junior and Best Score.

More pressingly, it also took the top prizes, including Best Picture, Best Director for the up-until-now-always-a-bridesmaid Christopher Nolan, and Best Actor for Cillian Murphy. (Murphy, who has been one of the best and most varied actors across film and television for decades, could not deserve his win more.)

There was Yorgos Lanthimos’s audaciously funny cyberpunk sex allegory Poor Things, which took a trifecta of craft awards (make-up, production design, and costume) before scooping Emma Stone a Best Actress statue; and The Zone of Interest, a formalist which was the first British film to take Best International Feature along with a well-deserved Sound Design win.

There was, in Glazer’s courageous speech, an acknowledgement of the brutality of the Israel/Palestine conflict, one which saw protesters delay the start of the ceremony on the streets of LA outside. Glazer and Glazer alone spoke directly about the conflict onstage; given The Zone of Interest’s subject matter, it was both fitting and honourable to do so.

It was, on one hand, heartbreaking to see Martin Scorsese and his epic masterpiece Killers of the Flower Moon go home with zero wins – particularly for the majestic and talented Lily Gladstone for Best Actress. But equally it was delightful to see the low-budget VFX team for Japan’s Toho Studios take home Best Visual Effects for Godzilla Minus One, or for Anatomy of a Fall to grab Best Original Screenplay in the face of much larger productions.

Disagree with certain choices though I may, this year’s Oscars were a shockingly vast improvement on previous versions, both in presentation and in decision-making. I don’t want to speak too soon, but maybe this really is Hollywood’s biggest night.
topics: Academy Awards, Film, Oscars

title: Robert Downey Jr’s redemption story is the stuff of Hollywood miracles
body:
It was a solid, credible, sensible Oscars (bar Lily. Oh, Lily!) but I personally like my awards season with a little more raw emotion. A lot more heart. So, thank God for the man who brought it early doors, his beautifully dispassionate acceptance speech belying the significance of the moment.

“I’d like to thank my terrible childhood,” said Robert Downey Jr of his expected win for Best Supporting Actor in Oppenheimer. “And the Academy. In that order.” We all laughed. “I’d like to thank my veterinarian. I mean, wife, Susan Downey,” he continued. “She found me a snarling rescue pet and loved me back to life.” And we laughed some more.

It was the best kind of laughter – you know, it comes from your mouth while tears erupt out of your eyes.

You see, his deadpan delivery was summoned from truth. Brutal, gnarly truth, obviously. Because it was something of a miracle for him to be stood there at all. The kind of unbelievable story arc that you only find in the movies, funnily enough.

That childhood? His dad, filmmaker Robert Downey Sr, once admitted to a “terrible, stupid mistake” in letting his son smoke a joint at the age of six. By the time Jr. was making his name in Hollywood, addiction was holding him hostage.

The mid-late-90s were marked by several arrests and publicised drug issues before he was sent to prison in ’99. In the courtroom he said of his addiction: “It’s like I’ve got a shotgun in my mouth, with my finger on the trigger – and I like the taste of the gun metal.”

Upon release, Downey Jr was cast as the love interest in Ally McBeal and then given the boot after yet another arrest. Later he’d say, “It was my lowest point in terms of addictions…I didn’t give a f**k whether I ever acted again.”

And we know how this story normally goes, right? We can all list the actors, the writers, the musicians, the greats, who’ve been caught in the jaws of addiction. Their flesh chewed through right down to the bone, their escape always-thwarted. A rollcall of names and shared tragedies, a list of loss we can barely comprehend.

But then, in 2003, the year he met his wife, Downey Jr got sober. He simply (and I’m sure not-simply) realised, “I don’t think I can continue doing this.” Within five years he was on our screens as Tony Stark in Iron Man, kick-starting the multi-(multi)-billion-dollar Marvel Cinematic Universe (even though execs hadn’t been so keen on him initially).

The world fell in love with Tony Stark, the selfish, egotistical ex-playboy. And the character who famously had heart issues ended up giving the MCU its soul and yes, its pounding, swelling heart. Here was a character who went on a journey worthy of, well, Robert Downey Jr.

When Downey Jr/Stark finally hung up his heart in 2019, speculation was rife about what would come next. Many post-superhero-era actors dream of the big serious award-seducing with the big serious award-seducing director; not all of them get it. Many don’t. Even Downey Jr’s impressive early dramatic work couldn’t guarantee a wiped-clean slate years on. But it never seemed out of reach. His trajectory had already been so remarkable.

And so it was that he didn’t just land the role of Lewis Strauss in Oppenheimer, but that he found himself stood, in front of his peers, on the biggest stage in the world, shaking off some very boring ill-judged jokes from host Jimmy Kimmel, to take home his very first Oscar.

Still, why exactly was I crying – and laughing, but mainly crying? As much as I’m sure Robert Downey Jr would resist becoming his addiction, I can’t shake the feeling that his “30 years of dependency, depravity, and despair,” gave him rare roots in humanity and empathy. That this is what penetrates the screen each time.

He knows what you can win, and what you can lose. The darkness that can swallow you. And surely, when you’ve been face down in the real stakes of a life, it never leaves you. Even when you get up, put on a nice suit and smile at the world with your cheeks clean and pink.

Now, his name sits alongside not the men we’ve lost, but the ones that were saved. That saved themselves. And made something beautiful, a new life, from what others only saw as wreckage.

(PS: I, we all, love you 3000).
topics: Actors, Addiction, Marvel Cinematic Universe, Oscars

title: Holly Humberstone, Manchester review: A star still finding her sound
body:
The singer-songwriter is skilled at trying on different stylistic hats, but she has yet to find one that truly fits

By now, Holly Humberstone’s preoccupation with places is well established; the title of last October’s debut album, Paint My Bedroom Black, suggested she believed in the importance of some feng shui when making an emotional restart. But even before that, she was lamenting the loneliness of stop-gap house shares on her 2021 EP The Walls Are Way Too Thin, a release on which tracks like “Haunted House” expressed her penchant for finding poetry in her immediate surroundings.

You wonder whether rooms like the one she has sold out tonight at Manchester’s Albert Hall will prove similarly inspiring, especially given that she’s been filling venues like this for a couple of years now. Winning the Rising Star award at the Brits in 2022 bestowed upon her the sort of profile that allowed her to pack out the likes of Brixton Academy, but you have to have the songs if you want to stay there. The gusto with which her lyrics are roared back at her in the atmospheric surrounds of the Albert Hall’s old Wesleyan chapel suggests she’s carved out a proper fanbase, emotionally committed and in it for the long haul.

It’s not difficult to understand why – her lyrics are earnest and forthright, and expressive of how readily teenage angst spills over into young adulthood.

As somebody born in the final fortnight of the 20th century, she has an astute handle on her generation’s struggle with the social media-fuelled imbalance between expectations and reality. “Cocoon” chronicles a depression-fuelled retreat into binge-watching The OC, “Kissing in Swimming Pools” pines for a world in which intimacy is guaranteed, and “Elvis Impersonators” nods to one of her key influences, Phoebe Bridgers, admitting that tour stops in Japan, thousands of miles from home, do not offer the kind of emotional refuge that she might have hoped for.

The spectre of Bridgers looms large over Humberstone’s songwriting. She is adept at mining her inner life for emotional currency. Also an influence is her one-time co-writer, Matty Healy of The 1975, in the sense that she sets her lyricism to music that is heavily in hock to pop-rock polish.

Singalong choruses that cast Humberstone as a guitar-wielding troubadour are cannily deployed (“Dive”). But she also dabbles in unremarkable indie R&B on tracks like “London Is Lonely” and “Girl”. In the set closer “Ghost Me” she unpacks the suddenness of her rise to fame with real wit, as she compares herself to the title character from The Truman Show, which makes it all the more a shame that the track is a folk-pop anthem-by-numbers in the mould of Mumford & Sons or The Lumineers.

It all adds up to Humberstone being skilled at trying on different stylistic hats, but the sense you get is that she has yet to find one that truly fits. In the fullness of time, will she settle into purveying breezy pop like “Sleep Tight”, or embrace acoustic confessionals like “Friendly Fire”? She’s won awards and sold out tours on the back of her lyrical identity, but perhaps she needs a clear musical one to go with it.

Touring to 16 March
topics: Gig Reviews, Live Music, Music Reviews

title: Love Rat review: Sally Lindsay is marvellous as a romance scam victim
body:
The ex-Coronation Street star was convincing as a con victim struggling with mid-life loneliness

There weren’t many twists in part one of Love Rat – not unless you were naïve tourist Emma (Sally Lindsay). At the conclusion of the gripping first episode of this four-part holiday thriller, she was shocked to discover there was more to her (clearly massively suspicious) new boyfriend Niko (Gerald Kyd) than met the eye. Or, more precisely, there was a lot less to him – and his wallet – than she had first believed.

Because while Niko was posing as the suave owner of the hotel in Cyprus where Emma had been enjoying a much-needed getaway as she recovered from a cratering marriage, he turned out to be nothing of the sort.

He was a romantic scam artist who had seduced Emma with a fantasy lifestyle and then smoothly separated his victim from her life savings – just to tide him over while he waited for a cheque to clear, he claimed. Instead, it was he who cleared off, after one final snog with Emma at the end of a instalment that combined cheesy thrills with an intriguing portrait of middle-age heartache.

Niko was obviously a wrong ‘un; any more red flags, and Emma would have needed sunglasses. So it stretched credibility just a tad that she would not be at least slightly dubious about his Instagram-perfect life.

He had a beautiful house and was always kind and generous – surely it was too good to be true (that incredible stubble should have sent alarms chiming for starters). But Emma, coming out of a shaky marriage to beleaguered Pete (Neil Morrissey), was desperate for love – and Niko ruthlessly exploited that need.

Sally Lindsay is best known as Coronation Street’s Shelley Unwin and there was a time when a stint on Corrie would condemn an actor to a lifetime of soaps. But, with Suranne Jones and Sarah Lancashire having used stints in Weatherfield as springboards into glittering careers in high-end TV drama, that is no longer the case. Lindsay was convincing as a woman struggling with mid-life loneliness.

As the debonair Niko, Kyd was just as persuasive – his performance combined charm with a subtle yet ever-present iffiness. He was never sleazy, just consistently sleaze-adjacent. You could see how his puppy-eyed millionaire routine would hypnotise someone as lost as Emma – even though he was plainly selling her a fantasy.

The one left drawing the short straw was Morrissey as Emma’s sad-sack ex. The details were left vague, but she had hurt him in the past, and he was still scraping the fragments of his dignity off the floor.

It was a thankless part for Morrissey – all he had to do was sound miserable at the other end of a phone line from Emma – and, unlike Lindsay and Kyd, he didn’t even get a free holiday in the sun. Nor did the solid Imogen King as Emma’s estranged daughter Susie.

Romance scams have been a hot topic since Netflix’s hit documentary The Tinder Swindler, so Love Rat hardly broke new ground. But Lindsay excelled as a woman fed up with life who just needed to catch a break for once. And Niko, with his subtle smarm, made the perfect villain.

As the end credits rolled, he seemed to have successfully vanished into the Cypriot sunset with Emma’s savings. However, three episodes of Love Rat remain, so the story would appear to have plenty of road left.

It was off to a solid start, and many viewers will want to stick with it, if only in the hope that Emma is reunited with her money and Nasty Niko gets his deserved comeuppance.

Love Rat continues on Channel 5 tomorrow at 9pm.
topics: Channel 5, TV Reviews

title: I’ve used bitcoin to create a million-pound pension pot – this is how I did it
body:
'I’ve seen my net worth plummet in the time it took to do the washing up,' says Joe, 37. He tells i why he held his nerve - and got rich, when others lost everything

The price of the world’s largest cryptocurrency, bitcoin, this month, briefly hit a new all-time high, where a single bitcoin was worth more than $69,000. Since its creation in 2009, it has fluctuated wildly, investors have lost their life savings, and others have become millionaires. Joe*, 37, from London, used to work in marketing for a tech company, and is now sitting on seven-figure bitcoin wealth. Here, he tells i how he did it. He has remained anonymous, to protect his security.

I first heard about bitcoin in 2011 on Twitter, and started thinking about buying it in 2013. At first, I wasn’t quite sure if it was going to work, but I liked the idea behind it. We’d gone through the 2008 financial crisis, and after that there wasn’t a banking system that I felt I could put my savings into which I trusted. I had lost faith (and I felt that inflation was a stealth tax).

I did a lot of reading before I did anything relating to cryptocurrency, and did six months of learning to work out whether bitcoin was viable, whether it was something I could trust putting my money into for a long period of time.

I started off small – a few hundred pounds here or there – and saw it fluctuate wildly and go down to below my buying price. I waited it out, to see if it would recover, and eventually it did. I’d watched bitcoin go through the doldrums, and through the depression we had for a couple of years, when nobody thought it was going to survive. In 2016, I finally decided to go all-in and invest my savings, around £15,000.

Throughout, friends and family were encouraging me to sell. I mean, there’s an entire website dedicated to all the articles printed which declare bitcoin to be dead – thousands of articles saying it’s pointless, it’s a Ponzi scheme, it’s all over.

There are a lot of naysayers, which I understand because there are a lot of charlatans and scammers, who cause issues. And there are people who get hurt by bitcoin, but I think it’s because their timeframe isn’t long enough, and they’ve not held their nerve. I’ve been doing the washing up and watched my net worth plummet by half by the time I get to the last dish.

Then during Covid, the markets tanked. But by that point, I’d been through these fluctuations so many times – bitcoin dropping by 30 per cent in one day – that I knew it would recover. I became a bit hardened to the worry, and would just turn my laptop off, or not check my phone for a bit. One night recently, for example, the price of one bitcoin was £69k (an all-time high) and went down to £60k over the course of a couple of hours. You come to expect these kinds of movements and, actually, I’m morbidly fascinated by them.

For a while, in 2018, I was daytrading bitcoin – buying and selling crypto assets. Early on, though, I thought I was clever and tried to time the selling of stock so I could buy it back lower and get more bitcoins – but I messed it up. I lost hundreds of thousands of pounds, so I stopped doing that. Now I just see bitcoin as a long-term investment.

I also spent some time listening in on a chat-room of people with way more crypto than I had, to understand how they were operating. It helped me pick up a few things from people who’d been in it longer than me, and how I shouldn’t get overwhelmed and emotional.

I now have low seven figures worth of bitcoin. I see it as my pension. For a while, I had close to 100 per cent of my net worth in bitcoin but when my initial investment became 10 per cent of my overall balance, I felt it was important to take some out, so I could live for the next few years and not worry about day-to-day price movements if it cuts in half.

I say to other people who have to pay rent, meet the mortgage or have dependents, that if they make good money, they should take a little bit out – at least the initial investment. Then you’re playing with gains, as opposed to loss.

There’s a temptation when your bitcoin picks up, to go out and buy a flashy car but I know that the moment I start to get excited, I have to hold back. The most expensive thing I’ve bought with bitcoin is a second-hand Golf. You see influencers on Instagram and Tik Tok, and they’re all telling you to follow their trading strategy, and they’re driving amazing cars and living it up in Dubai, but it’s dangerous to look to an online crypto guru to tell you what to do, how to play the markets. Do your own research, and don’t get your information from those social media platforms because a lot of it is just hype and noise.

I have thought about going to live in a country where cryptocurrency is tax free, like Portugal, or a country like El Salvador, which is trying to attract investors to go over there – but I don’t really want to live in either of those places. It would make sense for the British government to be amenable to people like me so we can keep our wealth in the country. It’s attractive to go elsewhere when other governments are approaching crypto differently.

It’s not been easy to get to this point, although of course there’s some luck involved, too. I still get people telling me to sell, but there aren’t many people to give me their views as I don’t advertise my situation to anyone beyond my closest family and friends. You’ve got to think about security, as there all these horrible stories about people with weak passwords or getting lax with security being hacked. You have to be so careful because you’re your own bank, there’s no third party in this, no insurance if anything goes wrong. If something goes wrong, it goes very wrong.

I don’t tend to give anyone advice because they get freaked out when the price moves, and it can put the fear of God into them. But if you do it, understand properly what you are investing in, and then expect that the day you buy the bitcoin, it will halve in value. Start with a little bit, maybe two per cent of your net worth, and forget about it for five years. The likelihood is it’ll be 10 or 15 per cent of your net worth by then.

I believe bitcoin is going nowhere, and in the next year we won’t be able to avoid it. The demand is massively outstripping supply, and there are going to be a lot of people popping up with expensive cars and houses rubbing all the naysayers’ noses in it.
topics: Bitcoin, Cryptocurrency, Features, Lifestyle, Money

title: I want to leave my bullying family business – but I’m trapped by the security
body:
As i's Agony Uncle, Kenny Mammarella-D’Cruz - who has spent two decades listening to men talk about their feelings - gives his advice on toxic family relationships

Kenny Mammarella-D’Cruz, i’s new agony uncle, advises a man that feels trapped in a family business

I’ve been living my life to please my family and keep up appearances.

I want to leave my family business, with its bullying ways, but I feel trapped by the security and I don’t want to let them down.

James, 35

How hard it must be to balance out the conflicting emotions from your situation, which might include guilt at how you feel, frustration at your lack of autonomy, resentment that you’ve been groomed for greatness and gratitude at not having to start at the bottom of any career ladder like your peers – and the lifestyle this affords you.

Many people born into a family business, especially when your parents or grandparents have started something innovative that’s brought your family out of poverty and often helped the wider community, are left in a predicament. On the one hand, how do you live up to the expectation that you’ll be like your parents or grandparents and share the same values to continue their work in a very different world?

On the other hand, you might find yourself questioning whether you’re allowed to follow different ideas, values and ways of operating? Are you ‘allowed’ to do better than your parents or grandparents in business? On some level, we want the blessing of our elders and being a successful individual in your own right can feel like a betrayal of your family.

It’s worth identifying exactly the feelings that this pressure imposes upon you. Do you feel restricted in how you represent yourself and are seen in public? Do you feel you ‘‘‘should’ wear certain clothes? You also might feel yourself questioning whether your family’s love is conditional. This all adds a sense of obligation to life; I worked with a minor aristocrat who temporarily lived abroad to explore who he really is and escape societal pressures and family expectations.

However, I wonder how much of this burden – which I have no doubt feels incredibly weighty – might be in your head, rather than coming from your family. The only way to find out is by talking to them openly and honestly. Keep in my mind that gratitude and feeling indebted are different emotions: gratitude comes with power to be free, without being a martyr or feeling owned by your family, or the business.

I’ve known many families who want the best for their children, and want to give them the chance to lead the family empire, presuming that is what they will want. What might be a dream come true for one generation can be quite the opposite for another. For example, older generations were respected for workaholism, while you might prioritise being available for your partner and children, if and when you have them, for playing games and bedtime stories – even the school run.

Before having an open discussion with your family, ask yourself some questions: what are your needs? How do you wish to live life? Where is your life being compromised? Beyond wealth and power, what do you want? It’s possible that you might need a break from the norm to take stock and look at life from the outside – and decide whether running the family business is a fit or not.

What makes this complicated is that the issues won’t simply be financial, but related to family dynamics. What part of the family script have you inherited? How can you exist within this script, or update the script? You might need to consider your own values so you can be true to yourself. Your situation is about the family beliefs that we are brought up with, which goes beyond standard people-pleasing, and you might find it helpful to see the world without looking through family lenses. Work out what values are important for you.

You mention the bullying ways that seem endemic within the business. Older generations built their empires in ways that seem toxic today, with ruthless decisions and bullying, leading with fear rather than listening and responding. Both business and society have evolved.

Modern leaders enjoy listening, collaborating and empowering others in a way that is less hierarchical, and a lot more responsive. Your family organisation may be in need of this kind of leadership, with you leading the change, and welcome your needs and terms to have you stay in the business.

If, after speaking to your family – and, crucially, listening to what they say – you decide the family business isn’t for you then respectfully call the board together, as adults, to explore options for the future. Get together as a family and look at the bigger picture, by celebrating all that your parents or grandparents have achieved.

Sometimes older generations need acknowledgement before they can let go and set themselves – and everyone else – free. You might find yourself in a position of finding a replacement for yourself: from within the family, or perhaps someone free of family ties. It might be that the leadership goes from one person to a group of individuals.

Unless your family is very toxic, you’ll probably have a wealth of opportunities to start your own business. Maybe your family wealth has given you a safety net so you can be truly free and do some good within the world without the financial restrictions felt by many. Do remember, you have the option of following your heart, whether within the family business or outside of it.
topics: Bullying, Family, Features, Work

title: I was a fly tipper – now I’ve joined the squad fighting to keep our streets clean
body:
Illegal dumping is blighting our neighbourhoods. Eleanor Peake goes on patrol with a London council team, who explain why it's a growing issue

“Stop him,” shouts Jane Callard, as she jumps to open the car door. We are 20 minutes into our patrol and Callard has already caught a fly-tipper red-handed. Except he isn’t throwing rubbish, he is urinating. “We see this constantly,” she turns to tell me.

Peeing, I learn, counts as littering, and is well within the council enforcement officers’ remit. Luckily for the young man, who was staggering along the street at 10am on a Tuesday, it is raining. “We have to see a puddle on the floor to fine someone for urinating. If it’s raining, we have no evidence.”

Callard hates litter. Even before she joined Newham’s Fly-tipping Enforcement team five years ago, she’d spot it wherever she went. In bin bags by a lamp post; some plastic bottles in a ditch, McDonald’s wrappers on the side of the road.

These days, her keen eye has only got keener. On our two-hour patrol through the east London borough of Newham, we see two men peeing, five abandoned oil barrels, a fridge, several discarded rubbish bags, and four bin bags full of loft insulation.

Callard and her patrol partner Shane Passfield have seen it all. “We see a lot of cannabis farms,” Passfield tells me. “Usually they will take the buds off the plants and then throw the rest on the street once they have abandoned the growing property.” They tell me about the brothel behind a local supermarket that leaves bags of condoms and tissues on the street.

As we get out of the car to inspect the bin bags that have been flung into a hedge, Passfield has a hunch. “This insulation looks like it has been taken out of a loft to make way for a cannabis farm.” He sighs. “Or it could be builders have ditched it.”

The incriminating bin bags are swiftly stickered with one of Passfield’s “Environmental Crime Scene” labels. “I hate bags like this,” says Callard. “It’s just so lazy.”

These black bin liners were discovered in one of Newham’s fly-tipping hotspots. “It happens a lot on the road because there is no CCTV,” Callard says. “If there was CCTV, we would go back to the office and investigate, and try to prosecute.”

Fly-tipping is on the rise at a staggering rate. The number of fly-tipping reports in England has increased by 13 per cent over the past four years. In London, this is even higher: in Tower Hamlets, there was a 93 per cent increase in incidents. In Barnet and Westminster, fly-tipping increased by 65 per cent and 64 per cent. In the latter, reports went up from 18,749 to 30,737.

In Newham, Callard, 51, and Passfield, 36, have some of the lowest rates in London. Their incident reports fell by 32 per cent in the same period, beaten only by Bexely, which fell by 29 per cent. “We are known as Tango and Cash,” Passfield tells me.

Last year, the pair discovered barrels of animal fat left in the middle of the road. “It was blocking cars and business so that was urgent,” says Passfield. Within half an hour, the team had organised a grab lorry to arrive and remove the lard. The pair estimate that 10 per cent of their patrol is spent responding to reports by residents. The rest is focused on keeping an ear to the ground and looking out for sporadic incidents. It takes a trained eye to keep up.

Callard lives down the road from the enforcement office and patrols the borough every morning, five days a week. Sometimes, she has been forced to prosecute her own neighbours. “It’s funny because a year later they will stop their car and say: ‘Hi Jane, how’s it going?’ As if nothing happened,” she laughs. Newham also happens to be my borough.

On my busy road, fly-tipping doesn’t seem to be that common. Passfield tells me this is typical. “Areas where there are lots of flats are usually spotless,” he says. Instead of leaving mattresses on the street, residents in my block leave their unwanted items in the designated bin area, inside the building. I left a mattress there recently and paid £25 for it to be collected by the council. The nearby canal path is occasionally sprinkled with debris. A Tesco trolley here and there.

The real problem areas are high streets and back streets. “It’s a place with a transient population,” says Passfield. That means streets with homes above shops or roads with a high turnover of residents.

This is a growing issue. Thanks to the rental crisis, thousands of London residents are only able to live in a property on a short-term basis before being evicted or priced out. James Asser, a Newham councillor, is aware of the problem. “High turnover of residents makes it very difficult to embed into a community. If you’re embedded in your community, you will naturally have greater commitment to it and be less likely to dump rubbish,” he says.

It isn’t just about being a bad citizen. This type of fly-tipper might not be aware of local council rules; there might be a language barrier, or renters might be beholden to a landlord who hasn’t provided renters with accurate waste information. Terrace houses that home over six people can apply for larger bins, but many are unaware they can upgrade from 240 litres to 360 litres. But as Callard reminds me: “Everyone is legally responsible for their waste.”

Then there is the cost of waste collection. Asser assures me that this isn’t impacting fly-tipping rates. “We did a one-year experiment where we suspended the £25 payment and it made no difference. We did see the number of bookings go up, but we also saw a drop in the number of people going to the recycling centre and charities reported there was a drop in people bringing donations of furniture,” he says.

“If you’re the kind of responsible person that will get rid of their waste sensibly, then you will take the free collection.
