But if you’re not that person, I don’t think you’re suddenly going for a booking just because it’s now free. You still have to go through the process of booking and filling in the form.”

As a student at a London university in 2015, I was one of these unsensible people. Our five-person flat was on a busy high street road. We had no big green bins or any form of waste disposal. Our landlord assured us that we could leave our black bin bags by the public street bins just outside our door. At 19, and as part of the city’s transient population, we did just that. For a year we left our rubbish on the street. We had no idea this was fly-tipping, or even illegal until we received a big yellow fine of £400.

This is worryingly common. The campaign group Keep Britain Tidy found that half of people in the UK have left their rubbish next to a full bin. “Lots of people leave rubbish by full bins in the street because they think this is going to get collected,” says Passfield. “It’s illegal.”

Of course, it’s not just students and the ill-informed. There’s also the commercial fly-tipper; the type that tosses fridges in ditches, and even asbestos. “I have seen a lot of asbestos,” says Passfield. These types of tippers are usually tradesmen who might be clearing up after a job, or unlicensed waste collectors who charge cheap rates to bin items in car parks or dark alleyways. The most common place for fly-tipping in the UK is just off pavements and roads, making up 40 per cent of total incidents last year. “Years ago we had a car park with tons of waste that had been left. It took the council several days and cost £70,000,” says Passfield.

Fly-tipping levels spiked during the pandemic. “It was when council services were disrupted. It really came on our radar as a problem after that,” says Asser. But more recently, following the cost-of-living crisis and council cuts, the problem has worsened. “Councils are stretched in terms of the resources they’ve got available. 20 years ago, when money was less tight, this was less of an issue.”

Callard and Passfield used to be part of a team of 10. Now, it’s just them. In 2016, Passfield remembers days spent educating the public with leaflets and community outreach. “There was a restructuring in 2021, and the team for the borough was cut,” he says. “We used to have a police branch and we would organise sting operations.”

He remembers one particular incident, where they tricked an infamous unlicensed waste remover into meeting them in a quiet cul-de-sac and tried to arrest him. “Those options just aren’t there any more,” Asser tells me. “And at the same time, we have more people who can’t afford to get things removed and so the cheap option of the man with the van becomes very tempting.”

Things have changed a lot since then. Passfield started his career as a dustbin man and later joined the police force as a special constable. In his new job, he has kept his policeman’s presence. “I try to be clear and calm when dealing with the public,” he says. “I once had someone shake my hand after I fined them.”

During our drive, residents frequently approached us to complain. One East Ham business owner marched over as soon as he spotted us inspecting some abandoned oil barrels. “Catch them please,” he says. “I can’t leave my bins outside my business because people just fill them up as soon as I do.” He points to his shopfront down a quiet street. Every day his large industrial bins are being filled up by fly-tippers.

John Clark, 64 from Redbridge, knows this too well. “I own a nightclub and the car park is constantly targeted by fly-tippers,” he says. He has been left with fridges and mattresses, to the smaller bags of rubbish. “I have a big bin that we have had to put a lock on now. I have been fined several times by the council for someone else’s fly-tipping.”

Clark has reported the issue to his council countless times, and while the fly-tippers have occasionally been caught and fined, Clark has had to remove the items at his own cost. “I had to have the fridges taken away by a specialist contractor, and it cost me £110,” he says. The problem has got so bad in Redbridge that this year the council have raised the on-the-spot fine to £1000.

Back in Newham, Mondays are the busiest for Callard and Passfield. They drive around the borough, from East Ham to Stratford, recording everything that has been dumped on the street during the weekend’s festivities. After nightfall, the disposal team comes to collect it; prepared with heavy-duty removal equipment. Christmas time is even busier for the Newham pair. “It’s just trees everywhere you look,” says Callard.

Fighting fly-tipping is a complex puzzle. “It’s a bit of a jigsaw,” says Asser. “You have to tackle it in multiple ways. It’s a combination of reinforcement, for those people who are just determined to not do the right thing. And then there’s a bit of education too.”

For the transient fly-tipper, outreach work has been most effective. “We’ve been campaigning and explaining to people that putting a couple of bags on the street is fly-tipping. That has been having an impact.”

As the campaign moves forward, and rates continue to rise across the UK, Callard and Passfield will remain on the streets of east London. They will continue to drive out every morning to clear up the debris. “A lot of this job is getting people to understand the impact,” says Passfield. “To understand the impact it is having on the community.”
topics: Councils, Features, London, Pollution

title: We’re middle class and can’t afford our lives – but are too ashamed to admit it
body:
Since graduating to a more middle class way of life I've found that people are competitive, and so won't admit when they're skint, says Sam Delaney

When I was a kid, my mum was always worried about money. She was a single parent, raising four sons in a council house while working as a part-time secretary. It wasn’t easy and I remember her forever scribbling out little sums on the back of final demand letters, which would be strewn around the house. We always had food on the table but there was a sense of tension around money all of the time and unexpected bills would represent a full blown crisis.

One thing that my mum always had, though, was a support network of mates (mostly other single mums) who were in a similar predicament. They didn’t seem to feel any shame about their money worries: they were honest about them, they would share them liberally with each other, often with a sort of gallows humour. I think it helped my mum hugely.

As I graduated to a more middle class way of life in adulthood I found that people were less candid about their financial situations. There is a quiet competitiveness about the middle classes that make people more reluctant to open up about being skint. Which is a real shame because – as the stats show – we’re all worrying about money. The only difference is that some of us do it in private which, from my experience, only makes it scarier.

According to new research by MoneySupermarket and suicide prevention charity Campaign Against Living Miserably (CALM), 34 per cent of people don’t talk about their finances because they don’t want to feel judged, 33 per cent feel a sense of embarrassment and 30 per cent don’t share money worries as they don’t want to be an emotional burden to friends or family. And things are only getting worse: over half (52 percent) of the population are more worried about money than 12 months ago, with one in two people reporting the cost-of-living crisis is making them feel anxious.

This is familiar to me, I have carried financial anxiety from childhood to adulthood even though my material circumstances have improved. I’ve had times where I have been skint and times when I have felt relatively loaded but the anxiety has always been there either way. The most recent, and extreme, bout came in September 2022 around the time of Liz Truss’ mini budget.

The irony is that a few months previously, in the summer of 2022, I’d decided enough was enough. I’d finally decided to take control of my finances for the first time – before then I’d adopted a head-in-the-sand approach, navigating good times and bad with an ‘oh well, something’s bound to come up’ type attitude – but I told my wife we must get organised.

The cost of living crisis had been imposing a sense of financial unease on us for a while, with bills going up and the treats that make life worth living becoming less and less affordable. (My wife and I are both self-employed so our income can be unpredictable.)

We’d asked a broker to find us a new mortgage to bring down our massive monthly repayments. He told us he had a deal in the bag that would save us several hundred quid a month. It was a big relief. That was, until the mini-budget. The broker was back on the phone within 24 hours telling us that the offer had been withdrawn. The best deal he could now do represented a small increase on our previous repayments. We were back to square one. No, it was actually worse.

I felt helpless, frustrated, confused and overwhelmed. I struggled to sleep. I got snappy and irritable with my family. I cancelled social plans because I felt too grumpy (and skint) to see people. I became anxious and miserable. And, soon, I was passing these negative vibes onto my wife, who is usually the more level-headed half of our marriage. She could see how much I was freaking out and started to perceive our situation as worse than it probably was.

In reality, it was manageable. We made economies elsewhere, took on a bit more work and, eventually, life muddled along as it always does. We were lucky. I am aware that there are many people for whom the cost of living crisis is far more serious.

We never worried about feeding our kids. We didn’t have to switch the heating off. And the very fact that we had a mortgage, and a property that we ostensibly owned, gave us more security than millions of others. But many of us, irrespective of our jobs, are worrying about money. The middle classes are feeling squeezed.

So I’ve decided to revert back to the sort of honesty with which my mum always discussed money. If a pal wants to meet for lunch at a fancy spot, I have no qualms about telling them I can’t afford it. The other day a dentist offered me an expensive root canal to save a tooth. “Pull it out!” I said. “It’s cheaper and I don’t use that tooth much anyway!” It felt good (the honesty I mean, not the tooth being yanked out).

Maybe, aged 48, I have dropped the need to be perceived as rich and successful? Money impacts our self-esteem in a profound way. The amount we have in the bank can feel like a reflection of how well we are doing. So when we are struggling, we can tell ourselves that we are failing at life. Feelings of shame can overwhelm us and make us less likely to share our situation with others. Keeping these worries inside is only ever likely to compound them.

In the past I certainly didn’t even discuss my money worries with my wife because I didn’t want to burden her. She didn’t want to bring up concerns with me in case it triggered the anxiety that she knows has plagued me for years. It was like a conspiracy of silence. Meanwhile, I didn’t want to share my worries with my friends and family because I thought they might judge me. I didn’t want to feel as if I was falling behind.

But I’ve come to realise that by being honest about my own problems I can help others deal with their own. Some of us have it harder than others, but money plays a huge part in everyone’s mental health. The more we talk about that, the easier it can be for everyone.

title: How high earners can use new child benefit rules to boost their pension pot by £170k
body:
A parent on £75,000 a year could claim nearly £16,000 in child benefit payments by increasing their pension contributions

Parents earning £75,000 could gain £16,000 in child benefit payments while also leaving themselves nearly £170,000 better off in retirement after a rule change at the Budget, analysis shows.

Chancellor Jeremy Hunt surprised families in his speech last week by raising the threshold at which parents start being charged for claiming child benefit from £50,000 to £60,000, and removing the top salary when no child benefit is received to £80,000.

Analysis from wealth manager Quilter shows that a family with two young children, where one parent earns £75,000, could increase their pension contributions from £200 to £600 per month, and claim £15,931 over the 12-year period during which their children are eligible for child benefit payments.

By doing so, they could increase their pension pot by £167,364 at age 68, assuming a growth of 2 per cent after charges and inflation, according to Quilter’s calculations.

Such parents could gain because child benefit thresholds are calculated based on income after pension contributions. If someone increases their pension contributions they may fall below or closer to the income threshold.

“Parents often don’t realise that they can receive much more in child benefit payments by upping their pension contributions while also setting themselves up for a more prosperous retirement and taking advantage of the favourable tax relief available,” said Shaun Moore, tax and financial planning expert at Quilter.

“Although this does mean that someone has to increase how much they are saving for retirement, the benefits mean that the ultimate gain far outstrips the spend,” he added.

The calculations assume someone already has a £100,000 pension pot at the age of 40 and already contributes £200 every month. It also assumes that the children still have 12 years of child benefit payments available, based roughly on the average age that people have children.

Under existing child benefit rules, parents receive £24 a week for one child and £15.90 for each additional child, but those amounts are due to rise to £25.60 and £16.95 a week in April.

Under the current system, if one partner earns more than £50,000, child benefit starts being gradually withdrawn. If they earn £60,000, they do not receive any child benefit at all.

This means two parents earning £49,000 a year each would receive child benefit in full – but a household with one working parent or a single-income household earning more than £50,000 would have the benefit cut.

This threshold figure has not changed since 2013, despite childcare costs and the cost of living soaring over the past few years.

However, the Chancellor confirmed in Wednesday’s Budget he would address this “unfairness,” by initially increasing the charge threshold from £50,000 to £60,000 and eventually making it based on household income by April 2026.

He explained: “I confirm that from this April the high-income child benefit charge threshold will be raised from £50,000 to £60,000.

“That means no one earning under £60,000 will pay the charge, taking 170,000 families out of paying it altogether.”

In a second reform to the child benefit cap, Mr Hunt went on to pledge that the top of the taper at which the child benefit is withdrawn is rising from £60,000 to £80,000.

The initial changes will come in from April.
